speechtext: On the Orders of the Day being called:

In the absence of the right hon. the Prime Minister, I should like to ask the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce, whom we are very glad to see again in his seat, if the Government has had any communication with the Government of the United States in respect to the substance of an article which appears

in a Government organ, the Ottawa Citizen, of this date, entitled: 'Joint Waterway from Duluth to Atlantic Ocean; International Commission discusses plans at Washington and will bring project to attention of the Canadian Government.' I am not reading the whole article, but just a portion of it:
Washington, Jan. 25.-A project for the joint construction by the governments of the United States and Canada of a deep waterway for ocean-going steamers from Montreal to Duluth, Minn., has been inaugurated through the International Joint Commission, which has jurisdiction over the boundary waters of the two countries.
The discussions instituted through the International Joint Commission are the result of a recent conference in Washington, in which Secretary Bryan, Chairman James A. Tawney of the American section of the International Commission, and Senator Charles E. Townsend, of Michigan, participated.
It was arranged that the matter should be taken up first with the Canadian Government through the commission. Chairman Tawney will confer soon with T. Chase Casgrain, K.C., chairman of Canadian section.
The project for an ocean waterway from the head of navigation on lake Superior to the Atlantic has been agitated for many years. It was considered seriously at the time when President Taft entered into reciprocity negotiations with Canada.
Hon. GEO. E. FOSTER (Minister of Trade and Commerce): I have not been in as close communication with the Government lately as I could have wished, and in the absence of the Prime Minister I shall have to ask my hon. friend to repeat his question later when the Prime Minister comes in. I myself am not aware of any communication having been had.

Hon. GEO. E. FOSTER (Minister of Trade and Commerce): I am sure that the House would like to hear the following cablegram from Mr. Griffith to the right hon. the leader of the Government:
London, Jan. 26, 1914.
Rt. Hon. R. L. Borden,
Ottawa, Ont.
The funeral service for the late High Commissioner held in Westminster Abbey to-day was attended by representatives of Their Majesties the King and Queen, Queen Alexandra, the Duke of Connaught, Prince Arthur of Connaught, the Duchess of Albany, Princess Louise, and many members of His Majesty's Government. There were also represented a great number of the leading scientific, educational and other bodies, as well as the Royal Academies of Art and Music. Public sympathy was most marked. The event was a great tribute to Lord Strathcona's outstanding personality, and unmistakably betokened great
good-will toward the Dominion of Canada which he so long and so well represented.
(Sgd.) Griffith.

I wish to call the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) to an article that has appeared in a number of papers. I am reading from the Ottawa Free Press of Friday, January 16, which contains a statement alleged to have come from one Captain R. F. Clift, a member of the Dominion Wreck Commission. This article says:
Captain Clift narrowly escaped being a passenger himself on the ill-fated Cobequid, and in recalling with some satisfaction the trouble he had escaped by his last-minute change of plans, denounced with outspoken bitterness the folly of compelling vessels of the type of the Cobequid to travel by the St. John route through the Bay of Fundy in winter.
' It is nothing short of manslaughter, no, it is worse, it is murder,' he said, ' to compel vessels to traverse the Bay of Fundy at a season when such terrifying hurricanes are likely to crop up and when fogs make it almost impossible to be certain of a successful battle with the dangerous racing currents.
' The Bay of Fundy has a rise and fall of tide of thirty feet, the greatest in the world, and the waters swirl through it at a perilous speed, so that when lashed into fury by storm, and obscured by fog, a shipmaster has not a fighting chance.'
The people of St. John, the captain continued, had used every kind of political pull to get the Royal liners to call, and had tried to coerce Sir Thomas Shaughnessy into allowing the Canadian Pacific railway vessels to come to St. John, but Sir Thomas had replied: ' No, I absolutely refuse to imperil my ocean liners by allowing them to go into the Bay of Fundy, with its dangerous cross currents.'
' It is absolutely jeopardizing the lives of captain, passengers and crew to send them across the Bay of Fundy in winter,' concluded the commissioner, * and the captains only do so under protest and agains their judgment. Halifax is the safer winter port.'
I should like to know if this man, Captain R. F. Clift, is a member of the public service of the Dominion and an official of the Department of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. If so, I desire to ask if this matter has been called to his attention, and if he proposes to investigate it, and, I would say, bring this officer to account for making such libelous statements as are contained in this article,

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Captain Clift, whose opinions have been quoted by my hon. friend from Carleton, N.B., (Mr. Carvell) is not an official of the Marine and Fisheries De-

partment. He is a retired sailing master, as I understand, residing in Montreal. From time to time, for a good many years past, the Wreck Commissioner, in investigating wrecks on the St. Lawrence route, is assisted by two nautical assessors familiar with the conditions of navigation. The Wreck Commissioner has on several occasions called Captain Clift in for such purpose and he has acted in the capacity of a nautical assessor. But he is not an official of the department; he is not in the pay of the department. The impression, which, it would seem, he himself tries to create, that he is an official is entirely without foundation in fact. I had read the unfair and unjust statement to which the hon. gentleman refers, and, knowing what a slander it was against the Bay of Fundy, at once called the attention of the Board of Trade of St. John to the matter and suggested that it would be desirable that steps should be taken to place the facts fairly before the public. Inquiry has been made into the wreck of the Cobequid by the Wreck Commissioner, Captain Lindsay, assisted by two nautical assessors. I understand that the report and judgment of that court has been prepared and in a few days will be given to the public through the press. While I have no right to forestall the conclusions which the court has reached, yet, having followed the evidence given at the inquiry with a considerable degree of care, I venture to express the belief that it will be found that the Wreck 'Commissioners are not of opinion that the wreck was due to any inherent danger existing in the Bay of Fundy, but to other causes altogether.
I think it unfortunate, that, in connection with a disaster of this sort, any one should attempt to make capital against any special locality or any special waters over which navigation into Canada has to take place. Charges from time to time have been made with regard to the navigation of the Bay of Fundy. While there are dangers in the Bay of Fundy, as there are dangers to be found in all waters which ships navigate, yet I think it has been demonstrated in the past, time and again, that the dangers which exist in the Bay of Fundy are no greater than those which exist in many other navigable waters of the world. A good many years ago, when the late Senator Ellis was a member of this House, some charges of this character were made on the floor of	Parliament when	the	question
was being discussed of subsidizing
rMr. Hazen.]
steamers from Ports in Great Britain to Canada. This was in 1887 or 1888. Senator Ellis put upon the record of ' Hansard,' where it can be found by any one who is interested, a statement carefully prepared by the Board of Trade of St. John, showing the ships coming to and going from the Bay of Fundy and going in and out of the Port of St. John, and specifying the number [DOT] of casualties occurring over a long period of years. The facts demonstrated beyond question that the Bay of Fundy was not a particularly dangerous water to mariners, and that the casualties during a number of seasons occurring in the Bay of Fundy are less than the casualties in many other ports of the world, upon which no such attack was made. It would be improper for me to reflect on the dangers of navigation of the St. Lawrence; these also have been much exaggerated. Of late years, with the aids to navigation provided and the means taken so far as possible to develop the means of protection to the mariner, a very great improvement has been made. It will be found, I believe, if a comparison be made- and no one attacks the record of the St. Lawrence-that the record of the Bay of Fundy is quite equal, if not superior, as far as casualties are concerned, to the great St. Lawrence route from the sea to Quebec and on to Montreal.

Hon. Mr. HAZEN. I must bow at once to your decision, Mr. Speaker. But perhaps I may take a more fitting occasion to refer to the question raised by my hon. friend from Car-leton, N.B., which was a most proper one to ask. I must content myself now with saying that the casualty under discussion did not occur in the Bay of Fundy. I think that the inquiry by the Wreck Commissioner into the causes of the wreck of the Cobequid will be found to have been of the fullest possible character, and the result will be given to the public as soon as it is possible to do so.
On the Orders of the Day being called:

I invite the attention of the Postmaster

General to the condition of the mail service between Sackville, in Westmorland county, and the eastern portions of the county over the line of the New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island railway. I have just received a telegram from the eastern part of Westmorland, stating:
No train over this route since 19th. No mail 19th to 23rd. Mails now coming by team. Road could easily have been opened 23rd or 24th. Inquiries at railway office meet with no information given no remedy.
The railway referred to runs from Sackville to Cape Tormentine. It connects at certain seasons with a mail service to Prince Edward Island at Summerside. I would ask my hon. friend the Postmaster General if his attention has been called to the fact that the New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island railway is snowbound, that the mails have been interrupted since the 19th of this month. This is a very important section of the country, and naturally the people are very much interested in having a mail service. They have a daily mail service when the trains are in operation, but, apparently, they have no such mail service now.

These things very often come to the notice of the department. The unfortunate part of the matter is that although the Post Office Department has a contract with the railway companies to carry the mail, it has no means of forcing them to do what they ought to do under certain circumstances. In this case there is a standing order from the department at once to get out teams or employ other means of transportation for the purpose of taking proper care of the mails. The particular point to which my hon. friend refers has not been called to my attention, because, I suppose, the officers of the department have instructions to do at once the next best thing in order to ensure a proper delivery of the mails to the public and it will be done in this case.

On Friday last the
general manager of the Intercolonial railway sent notices to the newspapers of the Maritime provinces to the effect that the operation of twenty-three trains of the Intercolonial railway system, including the Ocean Limited, would be discontinued on Monday of this week, that is to-day. Has this matter come to the attention of the hon.
Minister of Railways and Canals, and, if so, have instructions been sent out cancelling any such order, and providing that the operation of the Ocean Limited be continued as heretofore? Has the hon. minister any knowledge as to the other trains in question, and if so, what trains running over the Intercolonial railway are to be discontinued?

I have
no knowledge of any twenty-three trains being taken off. The Ocean Limited is to continue to run, and I shall be able to inform the House to-morrow or the next day as to whether that train will continue to run during the next two months.
Do I understand the hon. minister to say he has no knowledge of the discontinuing of the twenty-three trains mentioned?
Yes.

Such an order went
out.
I never heard of it.

Consideration of the motion of Mr. H. F. McLeod for an Address to His Royal Highness the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the proposed amendment thereto of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, resumed from Friday, January 23.

Mr. Speaker, at the time of the adjournment, on Friday night, I was referring to the remarks the hon. Solicitor General had just made in regard to the policy adopted by the Senate in connection with the proposal of a grant towards the improvement of highways. The hon. Solicitor General contended, in good faith, no doubt, that the Senate had no right to amend the Bill which the House had passed, because, he said, in respect to a money Bill, to a Bill providing for the expenditure of a certain amount of money, the Senate cannot effect any amendments, additions, curtailments, or alter the nature and object of this Bill. He contended, moreover, that this Bill, though not intituled ' money Bill,' actually was a money Bill, and that the Senate should have kept their hands off it.
I said the other night, and I repeat it, there are dozens and dozens of eminent men in this House, and even in the Senate, who

certainly are as learned and as wise as the Solicitor General. The latter has, of course, the right to give his opinion; he is entitled to put almost absolute faith in the truth of his contentions; but he should leave the same freedom to others.
The leader of the Opposition in the Senate (Sir George Ross) is a man not to he trifled with. He has spent his life in parliaments, having long been the Prime Minister of his province, and to-day he has at his side to lend him a hand, men of long experience, men who are just as well acquainted as the Solicitor General with the laws and constitution of the country. I deny to the learned Solicitor General the right to deal in such high-handed fashion with whoever is of a different opinion, and to say: It is childish, it is laughable, it is preposterous! We have in this House large numbers of hon. gentlemen who have devoted their lives to study, who are perfectly in touch with our constitutional law and parliamentary usage, men who were members of this House long before the Solicitor General ever set his foot here, and who have disagreed with him. When I had an opportunity of addressing the House, the other night, I did so knowing where I stood, after looking up the points of law raised by him. and I was satisfied that he had no grounds justifying such sweeping conclusions as he arrived at. The learned Solicitor General should know one thing, and it is this: Whereas it is possible to make a nice little book with the things he knows, a very large one could be made out of what he ignores.
I have looked carefully into the Speech from the Throne. It appeared to me well prepared, well made, perfect in form, but terribly deficient in ideas. It contains nothing worth mentioning, save some expressions of sympathy to the Royal Family. Apart from that there is very little.
I smiled on reading the paragraph which heralded an increase in the number of senators. Why should the number of senators be increased previous to any increase in the membership of this House? As a rule, new senators are appointed only after the matter has been passed upon by the representatives of the people. In this instance, the first step is towards increasing the number of the senators. That is the way this Government goes about it. We style that putting the cart before the horse. Common sense would require that the number of members who express the will of the people should be first increased. In any case, I am anxious to see that Bill before the House.

I was surprised to find that the Speech from the Throne does not make any reference whatever to the navy, or to the thirty-five millions voted in spite of us during the last session. However, that legislation, according to hon. gentlemen opposite was the most important of all. It was so urgent that everything else had to be set aside to allow of its being passed. The hon. Solicitor General, as I stated a moment ago, is particularly well informed, and he endeavoured to make us believe that two and two make five. He it was who undertook to get a closure rule passed without submitting it previously to a committee for its overhauling and subsequent consideration by the House. Nothing of the kind was done. Nevertheless, that closure rule had been imagined for the purpose of getting the Navy Bill passed through the House. There is not a word in reference to it in the Speech from the Throne. I was greatly surprised to find that the members of the new Government had given up the navy which has caused so much trouble, and done so much harm. That navy, though, was a very desirable thing, since it was destined to save the British Empire. Now, there is not one word about it in the Speech from the Throne, not one.
The presence here of the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster), whom I greet with pleasure, suggests to me the idea that possibly he may have been recalled purposely to answer me. Where has he been ? No one answers. Was he in China, in Japan, in Australia, in Asia? No one has informed us of the fact. I am beginning to think that I am a very important man, considering that the most experienced, the most wary, the best informed man in the ranks of hon. gentlemen opposite has been recalled to answer me. Besides, it is stated by the big guns and in the Government organs, that the right hon. Prime Minister may go to London to represent us in Great Britain as High Commissioner. It is announced at the same time that the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) may proceed to London as our High Commissioner there. If all the big guns depart, it is not surprising that others should be recalled to take their places. As for me, I would be glad to keep the Hon. Mr. Rogers here; it is so amusing when he tries to gag us, that I am intent on retaining him in our midst.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what has become of the navy? What has become of that pressing necessity of a thirty-five million grant

to avoid an impending war with Germany? According to these hon. gentle en, it was of absolute necessity to forw rd those thirty-five millions, otherwise bankruptcy was staring England in the face. We were told that the Laurier navy was only tin-pot and no good. We could easily afford to grant those thirty-five millions, because the country was prosperous, they said. We have surpluses every year; it is an easy matter to forward thirty-five millions, to make a wedJing p e eat, wit '.out the country be ng any the worse for it In spite of the Opposition, in sp!e of :ts most determined efforts, the House voted those millions. The Bill was forward :d to the Senate. The hon. gentlemen in die other House were suppose to swallow that pill without much protest, provided it was slightly sugar-coated. But it is not such an easy matter to have the veterans of the Senate to swallow those pills. The man entrusted with the interests * f Canada v as no tyro; he said to the ministers: You have cried high and low, you have contended and repea ed in the House, and a number of your friends who are representatives of the people hove sta ed in every quarter: No navy without a previous consultation of the people; no expend!'ure for that object previous to the holding of a plebiscite which the people have to be called upon to vote. These members of the Cabinet hailing from the province of Quebec, all of them, were especially outspoken in their denunciations of the navy, that confounded navy, we Will not have anything to do with it, they would exclaim. We would rather cut off a hand first, start a revolution, if nec ssary, rather than have a navy previous to consulting the people.
By the time they get into Parliament, it is a grant for the navy that must be voted, and in quick time. But the hon. leader of the Senate (Sir George Ross) is not easily fooled. He stated to the hon. Prime Minister and his friends:	You
stated that there would be no Navy Bill passed previous to consulting the people; you are bound to stick to your word. What a pity, Mr. Speaker, that men who are entrusted with the affairs of a country as important as ours should thus change their minds from one day to the other. Is it not painful to have to acknowledge to the people that those who are in power are not keeping faith, make light of their promises as soon as they reach power, passed from one side of the House to the other, and accepted portfolios? Should a poor man act so, he would be dealt with pretty harshly.
The man who does not keep his word is not of much use. A public man has no right to do on the next day the opposite of what he promised to do the day previous.
I am glad to see that there is to be passed through the House a Bill in respect to the navy which is of a kind to secure my approval, I must admit, especially if its promoter is acting in good faith, as I presume he is. I mean the Bill introduced by Mr. Lesperance, of Montmagny, repealing the Navy Bill. If that hon. gentleman is acting in good faith, and is, as I believe, an honourable man, for he occupies a very high social position, I think I shall vote for the repeal of that Navy Bill. But, it may be objected, are you not stultifying yourself, after voting in support of that Navy Bill? Quite right, I voted in support of that measure, but at the time the country was prosperous, and we had millions galore, and besides we were told that it was necessary to pass such a measure and that the revenue was sufficient to meet any expenditure it would entail, without having any detrimental effect on the nation's credit.
But, in the meantime, matters have taken quite a different turn. The Minister of Finance has been forced to admit that we are facing a serious crisis, that our finances are greatly embarrassed, that commerce is no longer prospering, and that we must not think of changing the tariff because trade might suffer in consequence. I am wondering whether we are still in -a position to undergo the expenditure entailed by the upkeep of a war navy. Thus in supporting a Bill providing for the repeal of that Act, I would not be going against my past record. The financial conditions of the country having changed in the meantime, the German peril having vanished, order and peace being restored, why should we have a navy? Since we have no one to fear in any quarter, why should we uselessly spend so many millions?
I may decide to build for myself a mansion at a time when I have the means of doing' so. But supposing I undergo heavy losses on my stocks, or supposing I am under the necessity of making some unforeseen expenditure, have I not the right to say to my architect: Pray discontinue; I am short of funds, my financial position is not what it was when I made up my mind to build that mansion; I am no longer in a position to make such an outlay. Am I not just as justified to-day in voting for

the repeal of that Navy Bill, which the Government was not willing to carry out when the country's finances were still in their past state of buoyancy and we were in a position to do things such as those?
I am at a loss to say what the leader of my party is going to decide, what position he will advise us to take; but if I am free, as I usually am, if I am at liberty to act in accordance with my views and decision, I say to the hon. member for Montmagny that he may rely on my support. However, I must add: Be candid about it, and let not that Bill be mere trumpery.
The hon. member is usually straightforward in everything he does. If I have the assurance that this Bill is introduced in good faith and in the best interest of the country, I shall very likely support it.
The navy was a necessity in days gone by; all were agreed as to that. I just now see in his place the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster). Assuredly he is not the first comer. He as wejl as all his friends in 1909 joined hands with the Liberals to say to the then Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) it is necessary that we should build a navy. The Hon. Mr. Monk was the only one not to give his approval to that expression of policy. But I was pleased later on to hear that gentleman say: I was not in the House in 1909 at the time that resolution was voted, but had I been present I would have voted in its favour.
So it is certain, indisputable, that both political parties agreed at the time in approving what the Laurier Government did later on. I mean the purchase of two ships as models, and the carrying on of those naval building operations as fast as the financial conditions of the country allowed it.
But later on hon. gentlemen on the other side changed their minds. They said: If we let that Navy Bill pass, Mr. Laurier will remain in power so long as he wishes. There is a fine opportunity to embarrass him, to impede his progress; let us change our policy and try something else. So these gentlemen went to the people with altered views; as a result we were beaten . on that issue, mixed up with another of as great importance, that of reciprocity.
So I have the right to-day, in the presence of those facts, to say that hon. gentlemen on the other side have not been sincere in the stand they have taken; they have not kept their word; but when they have to appear once more before the people
[Mr. Lafortune. 1
for a renewal of their mandate, they will be called upon to render a strict account of their stewardship. The people will exact a true and faithful account, with vouchers attached. They will say. What have you done in connection with the navy? You had agreed never to spend a cent on that acount before submitting the matter to the electors, a promise which you have broken in voting those 35 millions.
I now pass on to another viewpoint. The hon. Solicitor General stated the other night that the Senate had not the right to effect that amendment to the Highways Bill. I have previously discussed that question, and I do not wish to cover once more the same ground. But I say that this House had no right to provide any expenditure for that purpose without specifying what highways were to be improved and where, what amounts were to be expended in the various provinces, in what manner and under whose authority. The majority of this House having refused to point out the particulars which I have just given, I say unhesitatingly that the Senate had undoubtedly the right to vote the amendment it did vote. And while listening to some hon. members during the last by-elections, who contended that if we had not the highways proposed by the House, it was the fault of the Liberal Senators, I could not help thinking that these gentlemen were in bad faith.
When it is stated to farmers: You did not get the highways promised you, or the money voted for those highways, but that is owing to the Senate, that is owing to the Liberals who refused to accede to the wish of the House of Commons, you did not get the protection you were entitled to because the Senate killed the Bill, I say such language is grossly insulting to the members of the Senate, for it is attributing to them motives and intentions which they did not have.
Then there is the appeal to the people. That famous plebiscite, not a word is said in reference to it in the Speech from the Throne, and the Nationalists themselves did not dare introduce a Bill providing for an appeal to the people However, they stated time and again, and on every hosting, that what they wanted was an appeal to the people. Not a single meeting was held in the course of the last election without the Nationalists exclaiming: We want an appeal to the people, we want a p'ebi-scite, and we shall oppose every demand made by the new Government if that de-

mand is not preceded by an appeal to the people.
Those gentlemen are in power since 1911; this is the year 1914, and it is the first time an effort is being made to redeem the pledges given in 1911.
Then as regards reciprocity, it was stated at the time: 'Let well enough alone.' The country was prosperous and as a result it was not necessary to make any changes, these gentlemen would say. To-day they are unable to say: ' Let well enough alone '; they must be content with saying: ' Let bad enough alone.' Public confidence is impaired, the cost of living is higher than formerly, and when the Government is called upon to apply a remedy, they answer: 'Let bad enough alone.' Hands off. That is a sign of a change in the times. Another sign is the fact that business is at a standstill and that the oldtime prosperity has disappeared. I see .that the hon. Minister of Finance stated, according to the Star of Saturday evening, that public opinion was not asking for a change in the tariff. To be able to express such a view, the minister must have sought that expression of public opinion among interested people, among manufacturers who are intent on continuing to draw those large dividends for themselves. But let the Minister of Finance come down to the people, let him inquire as to their views, and he will acknowledge that public opinion requires a change in the tariff. Let him inquire from the workingmen, from the farming class, he will soon find out that those two classes require more protection. But if he is content with gathering opinions among his own people, I dare say the result will be slightly different. I say that an enlightened public opinion requires a change in the tariff, in order to ensure greater protection to those who are entitled to it.
Mr. Speaker, at Montreal, the chambers of commerce, the most important business corporations are clamoring for the immediate building of the Georgian Bay canal, and I am surprised not to see any reference to it in the Speech from the Throne. How is it that so little deference is shown to the wishes of such an important community as that of the metropolis of Canada? There is not even an answer forthcoming to the numerous petitions which have been forwarded to the Government. Not a word, not even a refusal. Not a single reason given why the Government should not start at once the building of that canal. Reference is made to the appointment of a commission.
But for fifty years commissions have succeeded one another. For fifty years past, engineers and other experts have been at work investigating the possibility of building that canal, and in every instance favourable reports were made stating that such undertaking could not be dispensed with.
If there is no intention of carrying out the Laurier Act in regard to the building of ships, if it is not intended to continue spending 35 millions, which amount the House granted against our will, to be spent on the British navy, then let us build that canal; the funds which these gentlemen proposed to apply to the development of the navy, let us apply them to the building of that canal. No, these gentlemen are unwilling to do anything, except folding their arms and managing the Government.
When it comes to spending money on the militia, though, to have them drill and exercise, expenditure follows expenditure, trip follows trip, millions follow millions; there is no cheese-paring about it. The people are not consulted, and funds are spent lavishly. I say the Government is not accomplishing its duty in not listening to the appeal of the great corporations for the immediate construction of this canal.
Mr. Speaker, the other day I read in the papers that the Minister of Finance (Mr. White) had been under the necessity of negotiating a loan of 20 millions in London. The amount was large, and he had not succeeded. England advanced only ten millions. Just think of a country like Canada making to England a gift of 35 millions just before applying for a loan of 20 millions for the carrying out of urgent and necessary work within the Dominion. That is an odd situation. Is it not an humiliation for our country to have to beg for a loan of millions from Great Britain, while at the same time making her a gift of an equal amount, simply to show our generosity. Previous to buying a piano or a silk dress for one's wife, the baker, the grocer, the cobbler and all other suppliers of primary necessities should have been settled with.
I regret that the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell) should not be in his place; I would have something of interest to him to give out. I suppose he was appointed Minister of Agriculture because he knew something about agriculture, because he was conversant with the needs of the farming community. If he was here, I would enquire how it is that there is no reference whatever in the Speech from the Throne indicating the least concern for the

welfare of the farming community. It is nevertheless an important industry, and in this connection, I may refer to a crop on which the people in my county largely depend, I mean tobacco. Why should not the Government increase the rates on foreign tobaccos in order to further protect our Canadian growers. Our tobacco growers have to stand the competition of the foreign leaf. In days gone by the Government went to a large expenditure for the purpose of encouraging and developing the growing of Canadian tobacco, but the time has come to go a step further. A duty of five cents per pound should be imposed on the foreign leaf in order to help the farmers improve their methods as well as the soil itself. Those who are the least conversant with agriculture are aware that a depleted soil must be enriched. Our farmers might easily enough stand the competition- of foreign imports, if they were in a position to restore to the land its original fertility. It is necessary to restore to the soil those elements of which continuous cropping has deprived it, and -accordingly to buy potash which costs fifty dollars per ton. How do you expect farmers to go to such an expenditure without the Government coming to their assistance? Put on a further duty on foreign tobaccos imported from Havana, Kentucky, and other parts, in a word, on -all tobaccos competing with our home grown leaf.
That would enable our growers to maintain the soil in the proper state of fertility; instead of obtaining a thousand pounds an acre, they would possibly get fifteen hundred.
I was discussing the question with a Government official, a man of great ability and experience, of French origin, Mr. Char-land, chief of that section of the Department of Agriculture. He stated that if tobacco were properly grown in Canada, on well prepared land, it should yield
2,000	lbs. per acre, while it barely yields half that quantity. That is, he says, on -account of the deficiency in potash. Too much has been taken out of the soil by tobacco growing; it has to be enriched in that particular.
Now, the Minister of Agriculture has not a single word in the Speech from the Throne to show that he takes an interest in the farmer's welfare. Under the previous Administration, I had called the attention of the then Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fish-

er), to the necessity of encouraging agriculture. I had requested the establishment of experimental stations in the principal districts of the province. He had given me his word that he would promptly see to it. But to-day there is no reference whatever to -the subject. What would be the effect of the establishment of these stations from the point of view of the farmer? We have at Ottawa an experimental farm which has. cost millions. I am not finding fault with -that expenditure; but I do not say that there should be a dismemberment of the experimental farm. Farmers from the neighbouring districts in Ontario -and Quebec come y early to, the -central farm to collect new information. They reach Ottawa about noon, take lunch, and proceed to visit the farm. That takes two or -three hours time and they return home practically not knowing any more than if they had never visited the farm. I say that the best departure would be to decentralize the experimental farm by establishing experimental stations in the various rural districts of the province. A station might be established at Three Bivers to begin with, then at St. Hyacinthe in the districts of Richelieu, Joliette, Terrebonne, St. Francis and elsewhere. These stations would be illustration stations, for the purpose of putting object lessons under the eyes of the farmers, and imparting to them the information they are in need' of. I was disappointed to learn some time ago that the farmers of the province of Ontario had obtained 53,000 samples of seed grain last year, while the province of Quebec had applied for 9,000 only.
I wish, Mr. Speaker, that there were numerous stations for the distribution of that seed grain. Let the -samples be handled out at the church door on Sundays; let them be taken from house to house, if required, so that our farmers of the province of Quebec may be in a position to compete with those in the other provinces. We have strong arms, endurance -and a fertile soil; we have industrious and temperate men; they are not sufficiently protected in that respect. We are taking good care of the industrial classes of -the manufacturers, but the farmers are not looked after, they are a negligible quantity.
As regards by-elections, I - shall say a word concerning them presently. I would like the Government to take proper measures to enable our farmers to secure large profits. Experts should be appointed to visit the various counties, examine the

soil, find out what are its deficiencies, teach the proper methods of cultivation, the way to cut, dry and cure tobacco and so forth. Is that not what the Government did for butter and cheese factories? Why could we not do the same to help on tobacco growing? There is a complaint about people leaving the country and the cost of living increasing all the time; but apparently nobody suspects that all that is because farmers do not get the encouragement they are entitled to. Farmers abandon their farms, give up farming and come to the cities to take up trades. That is an very well, but what remedy is there for it ? The remedy is to give a greater measure of protection.. If we had an experienced Minister of Agriculture, anxious to get posted concerning the requirements of the situation by obtaining information from those who apply to him for protection, he would soon realize the truth of what I say.
The intention, it seems, is to increase the representation of cities and correspondingly diminish that of the country districts. Is that a proper means of encouraging farmers to remain on the land? It is contended that cities have not a sufficient number of representatives, and it is proposed to grant them larger representation at the detriment of the rural constituencies. Whether a member from Montreal represents 100,000 or 20,000 people, it does not make much difference, because the territory covered is the same; a city member may in five minutes call a meeting at a given place, and he may be sure that there will be thousands of electors to go and listen to him. But that is not my case, far from it, and in order to meet my constituents I must travel for weeks, or even a whole month, through rough roads, cross the Laurentian mountains, to inform them of what I have done or applied for in their interest.
It is not so much a question of population as a question of territory to be covered. Though my constituency has not a very large population, it is more difficult for me to get in touch with my electors than it is for the representative in a large city to communicate with his constituents. In the cities there are newspapers, there are public bodies, there are large corporations to keep the electors' posted. It takes them five minutes every morning to read the report of the world's progress; while 'my constituents, who are settled in the mountains, where it is difficult to have access, are ignorant half the time of what is going on elsewhere. A part of the world might disappear without their knowing it; the pope may die and they will find out only long after. There is no longer any talk about the Laurier navy, but they have not heard of it.
So I say that instead of increasing the representation of large cities, it should be left as it is, and the representation of rural districts remain where it is. But it is objected that the population of cities is increasing enormously. Take for instance the division of Maisonneuve, the population of which exceeds 100,000 souls. Well, my acquaintance with the hon. member for Maisonneuve is such as to permit me to state that he is not worrying over that. He is free to call meetings any day at some point or other of his constituency, and even two or three every day, and thus come in contact with his electors in very short time. In cities, an auto is summoned, committee rooms are visited in no time, and everybody is interviewed. But just go in the Lauren-tides with an auto, and keep me posted as to your progress. If you are anxious that the population of rural districts should diminish further, ill-use it as you are threatening to do by depriving it of its representation in Parliament. You will find that farms will be deserted, and that it will be difficult to get your supply of cabbages and radishes, for which even to-day you have to pay pretty high prices.
To my regret, I do not find anything in the Speech from the Throne in reference to a very opportune move which the Government should make. The hon. Mr. Foster, who has travelled over Europe, should have seen to that while he was in London; I mean the doing away with the embargo on Canadian cattle. The Speech from the Throne is silent on that point. It is all very fine to trade with the empire, but our cattle, after being shipped across the pond, are looked over and slaughtered on the wharves, under pretence of tuberculosis; people eat them all the same. In that way our best animals are sold at a sacrifice, under pretence of safeguarding the public health, but it sells cheaper per pound than if it was classed No. 1 when still on foot.
Have any steps been taken by the hon. Minister of Commerce (Mr. Foster) to do away with that state of things, with that embargo on Canadian cattle? Supposing we are told that the Laurier Government has not done anything to relieve the situation, do you think the people will be satisfied with such an answer? Do you think the

people have put in a new set of men without expecting an improvement in the condition of things? The people will soon realize that matters are not so well managed as they used to be. I shall charge the Government with sluggishness, with gross negligence in their dealings with the interests of the farming community, and for having neglected so far to take steps towards doing away with that embargo regulation affecting Canadian cattle. You propose granting 35 millions for the benefit of Great Britain, when your cattle are being slaughtered on the wharves in such fashion.
I am a farmer, I go in for the breeding of animals, and I say it is a crime to thus neglect taking steps towards putting an end to this state of things. You are aggrieved at seeing the people quit the land; protect us, help us, to begin with, and then we shall advise our children to stick to the homespun in preference to the silk hat of the city swell. But, in the first place, grant us the protection we are entitled to. We constitute 70 per cent of the population of the country, and that class which is so numerous is the very one which is ill-protected or not protected at all. We shall remain in the country, but under condition that you fulfil yourself your duty.
I charge with neglect the French-speaking members representing in the Cabinet the province of Quebec, for not making a better fight to obtain for us the measure of protection to which we are entitled. Not a line, not a word, absolutely nothing to show that they take some interest in the welfare of the farming class. For instance, petition after petition is forwarded, the newspapers in all the provinces are filled with expressions of opinion in regard to a world's fair to be held in Montreal. Resolutions passed by boards of trade, banks, insurance companies, large transAtlantic companies, etc., all go to state that, as a foregone conclusion, a world's fair should take place in Montreal. And there is not a word forthcoming from the ministers representing the province of Quebec; not a word showing that the Government are disposed to assist; they remain silent. It would seem that they hold portfolios with the firm resolve of avoiding all exertion, and that they are successful in attaining that object. Why do they not express their views as to the appropriateness of doing something in connection with the fiftieth anniversary of Confederation? One might think they have nothing to do with such matters. Well, I live on the
island of Montreal. We have there some highly valuable property. We have the right to know what will be the stand taken by the Government, what will be their position in regard to the fair.
Recently I read something in a newspaper which caused me much surprise; I could hardly believe my senses. It was stated that the right hon. Prime Minister, while in New York, had represented that he was not opposed to reciprocity. To read in a newspaper that the Prime Minister stated in New York, as being his ipse dixit, that he was not opposed to reciprocity, that comes rather as a surprise. And the right hon. Prime Minister has allowed that report to be circulated throughout the Dominion!
There is no one but knows that the Prime Minister has been the instigator of the movement against reciprocity. Good Heavens, what is this country we are living in! Who are the deceivers, and who are the deceived? The Prime Minister leaving uncontradicted the statement made in a newspaper that he was not opposed to reciprocity ! Well, Mr. Speaker, it is time for the sake of the dignity of this House that there should be a question put challenging these gentlemen to give an account of the view's attributed to them by newspapers.
There is still another question that puzzles me. I mean the famous Ne Temere Bill. Poor Mr. Laurier, many capital sins have been charged to you, when it was stated in Ontario: 'If the Ne Temere exists, it is Laurier's fault; he is unwilling that Canadian women of the Catholic faith shall marry Protestants. Put us in power, and I, Mr. Borden, will see to it that Protestants and Catholic intermarry.
How is it that nothing more is heard of it? Has it been forwarded to Jerusalem? During the last election the abolition of that Ne Temere decree had been promised. The intention was to legislate so as to do away with the enactments of the Ne Temere. The former Minister of Justice, Sir Allan Aylesworth, an eminent man, the most distinguished lawyer which I have ever met, gave his opinion concurrently with his leader, Sir Wilfrid Laurier. He stated that the constitution did not allow us to deal with that question, that it was not within the purview of the Dominion Parliament, but remained within the jurisdiction of the Provincial legislatures. Subsequently, the Hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), a former judge, an eminent jurist, was called upon to express an opinion, and he agreed

with the views of Sir Allan Aylesworth and Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
Those gentlemen were not satisfied with that. The matter had to be submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada, in order to ascertain whether the stand taken by such eminent authorities was well grounded. So the question was submitted to the Supreme Court, and it was decided once again that this House has no jurisdiction. But the matter was not allowed to drop and was carried before the Privy Council in England. Here again the opinion expressed by the former Minister of Justice and Sir Wilfrid Laurier was upheld. All that resulted in an expenditure of fifty thousand dollars for the country, while Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Sir Allan Aylesworth did not charge anything. In that way they succeeded in throwing away fifty thousand dollars, and the question is dead and buried.
There still remains the school question, that famous question. The Speech from the Throne does not say a single word about it, does not that make the least bit of reference to it, after all the talk on the matter we have had from the mouth of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). I would like to enquire from him, if I saw him in his place, whether	he is still	of a
humour to call Sir Wilfrid Laurier a renegade, a perjurer, an unworthy French Canadian, a coward, as he did on the hustings, taunting him for not having settled that question. He had not enough insults to hurl at the head of the former Prime Minister, branding him as a renegade, a knave. Later on, being questioned as to the intentions of the Government regarding that school question, he answered from his seat that this school question had been settled by the Greenway-Laurier agreement) an agreement which I concurred in. Was he sincere when he was slinging mud at the former Prime Minister, or was he sincere when he had succeeded in getting in the manger himself? The member for Jacques Cartier con-j demned the policy of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, adding that the policy propounded by Mr. Borden was even worse. That did not prevent him from accepting a portfolio in that same Government headed by Mr. Borden. True, he did not stay there very long after saying that he was bolted, riveted and padlocked to his ministerial seat. However, there was no padlock strong enough to retain him, and he unbolted, unriveted and unpadloeked himself; he
broke loose and ran away, and since has not been seen.
That is a well fettered man who runs away on the day following only. Since his resignation a very odd thing has been going on to my surprise; he has not in the meantime set foot in this House, and at the close of the year his friends passed a piece of legislation granting him his parliamentary indemnity. A man whom we meet every day in Montreal, on the street! He delivers lectures, but does not show up in the House. However, at the close of the session he gets his sessional indemnity all the same. We of the common fry, when we are absent one day, we are docked fifteen dollars; but as for this gentleman, he has the right to take it easy at the expense of the State, and at the close of the year small items will be inserted in the estimates for the benefit of those who have absented themselves. Well, I take exception to that way of managing things. You have sworn to protect the country's interests, to fulfil your duty as members of this House, to render your accounts and to give to Caesar whatever to Caesar is due. I deny you the right of pilfering the public monies and throwing them to the winds.
During our tenure of office, when we asked for subsidies amounting to $140,000,000, to meet the requirements of the country, we were branded as dishonest or incompetent administrators. But when hon. gentlemen opposite reach power, $140,000,000 are no longer sufficient. Last year it ran up to $250,000,000. What have you done with those millions? You have not a single word in the Speech from the Throne indicating the use they were put to. It may be objected that it is a little early to call for the estimates. That may be so; but should I wait a little longer, all will be dissipated, wasted.
I say that those men are not worthy of the confidence of the country, the confidence reposed in them by the people in 1911; they are not worthy of occupying seats on the Treasury benches. The Minister of Finance did not even state that he-proposed taking steps towards voiding the sale of that $300,000 property situated in Winnipeg, which has been given away for ten dollars.
Such are the deeds perpetrated in this twentieth century, in the capital of the Dominion. Have these hon. gentlemen lost their heads? One might come to that conclusion. No steps whatever have been

I am sorry I was not able to follow the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Lafortune) as fully as I would have liked. Perhaps in some respects I may be considered somewhat lucky. I do not wish to detain the House long, but there are a few things with which I wish to deal. In the first place, we have heard a great deal about emergency; whether there is an emergency or no emergency. It is all very well to argue about the relative positions of Germany and England, but whenever Great Britain has a serious rival on the sea we have an emergency, no matter who that rival may be. That being so, our responsibility must be apparent. Furthermore, I think that before we attempt to build a navy in this country we had better decide whether we are going to swim or fly. We all know that the question of an aerial fleet is a very prominent one in Europe to-day, and until we have decided whether we are going to swim or fly why not let Canada use Great Britain's plant, costing hundreds of millions of dollars, for building her warships. There is another consideration which every right-minded Canadian should think of. If we lay out this enormous amount of money on a plant to build vessels in Canada, there will be a large bill to pay annually to keep that plant up to date; otherwise it will become obsolete.
Another matter which has been brought up quite frequently is the Highways Bill. The right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition and his friends have been very eager to tell us that they do not want to hurt the Highways Bill. In other words, they want the child to cry but they are 12 .

afraid to whip it. That is the position they are in. The Senate, whether at the instigation of the right hon. leader of the Opposition or not, saw fit to change that Bill so that the Government could not accept it, and whether they so amended it for party reasons or otherwise, the fact remains that the Senate stands between the people and this great enterprise. The people do not wish to be deprived of this great benefit because of some technical opinion that some hon. gentlemen in this House may have. If we are to keep the people on the land in this country we must improve rural conditions, and any one who considers what the Highways Bill or a similar outlay properly expended as it has been in other countries would do for Canada, must admit that it would be a very great factor in keeping the people on the land. So long as they get good roads, it is a very small matter to the country what the opinions of any public man may be in reference to the effect of the Bill; and, while this proposal of the federal Government to assist the farmers of our country and the people who are interested in building roads is a new de-parure, it is one which is justified by the conditions in this country. Up to now the farmer has had to bear this great burden himself. But the burden has become too heavy for him, and hence the necessity of help from somewhere. One objection urged by hon. gentlemen opposite was: You would make political use of this Bill. I say that the federal Government, unless it declared these roads to be interprovincial roads, or in the general interests of Canada, could not go into any municipality or province and lay out one dollar of that money without an agreement on the part of the province and municipality as to how the money should be expended. The real trouble is that the measure is popular among the people, and hon. gentlemen opposite do not want us to get the credit. The right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition has told the country that his body politic is very sick or that it is seriously ailing. Let us see what kind of a prescription he suggests for a patient so seriously ill. It seems to me a very mild one, it is not heroic treatment anyway; in fact, he does not propose to prescribe anything at all. He says:
We regret to have to represent to Your Royal Highness that in the gracious speech with which you have met Parliament, whilst it is admitted that business is in a depressed condition, yet there is no indication of any intention on the part of your advisers to take any steps towards relieving such a situation.
He then called in the consultation the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael

Clark), and he has he same prescription whether the patient is sick or well-free trade. That is all he can recommend. If that is the kind of treatment this patient is going to receive at the hands of the leader of the Opposition and the prominent doctor whom he has called in, in consultation, I think the patient will have to get along without the help of these gentlemen. They tell us that there is a stringency in this country, but I say this: outside of the large cities and towns-where undoubtedly there are unemployed, perhaps because the towns have been overspeculating in building-the people, and I am speaking now for the farmers of Ontario, were never better off. Some years ago when our Liberal friends were in power hard times commenced in the country and stayed in the country-not only in the rural districts, but in the cities and towns; but the conditions to-day are entirely different. And these hard times cannot last for long when the rural districts are prosperous and making money as they are to-day. I am not able to give a correct statement as to the unemployed. The right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition estimated the number at 100,000; but his figures have been criticised by those who seem to know, who say they are away beyond the mark. What would it amount to if the figures were correct? It would simply mean that 100,000 people from England, Ireland, Scotland and other European countries came into Canada in three months in the year 1912-13, that is, at the rate of 1,200 a day or 400,000 a year. Everybody knows that these people cannot get employment the day they land here. They have to wait for positions. So this calamity of which we have heard so much does not really exist.
We have heard a great deal about the high cost of living. I know a man can live cheap because I have had to do so all my life. There is this to be said about the high cost; it is largely in the mode of people's living. I met a man the other day who said, ' Look what my bread costs me, it is terrible.' I said: 'You are a young man, about 35 years old, are you not? Well, when you were a boy wheat was $1.50 a bushel, and your mother used to make her own bread. But now wheat is $1 a bushel. Your wife makes you go out and buy your bread, and I will bet you the wife does not know where the clothes line and the scrubbing brush are in your own house.' Let us look these things squarely in the face. I will give you another instance. A man goes down town and pays 50 cents for a bushel of potatoes, and then pays $1 car-
[Mr. Broder.l
riage to get them home, so that they are costing him $1.50 a bushel. As long as the people have money to spend they will continue to raise the standard of living and increase their expenditures. There is only one remedy for that condition. My right hon. friend and the Government, if they wish, may pass all the resolutions they like in this House; but they cannot make that hen running around the barnyard lay one egg more; they can not add a pound to the bullock in the stall or the pig in the sty. The man who feeds these animals is the only one who can do that, the producer must do it, and if we get down to the producer we will remedy this trouble if the common sense of the people comes into play. My right hon. friend, the leader of the Opposition, speaking in Hamilton on the 29th November last, said that he was going to put the farmer on the free list. That is free food. The farmer has been working for hundreds of years and feeding the world cheaply but now that his pork and beef, his mutton, his poultry, his dairy produce, his tub of but ter and his grain are getting up a little in price my right hon. friend says:	Wo
must stop this, we must put him on the free list. I noticed that when ho got down to Montreal he modified his attitude; he was not so string upon'this question down there. He met a very cautious gentlemau down there, one who had made a bad bargain, the ex-Minister of Finance, and he told my right hon. friend that he must be very careful on this question .So he was, and he , was also careful in the resolution which he introduced here the other day.
The right hon. gentleman must realize that Canada is not producing the quantity of dairy produce that we might expect from it, an agricultural country. How can we justify this? Just last winter a gentleman sat down to his breakfast in the city of Ottawa and he had for his breakfast eggs from Russia, potatoes from Ireland, bacon from Denmark and butter from New Zealand. That should not happen in this country. There is only one remedy and that is to get the people on the land. I do not say that you must restrict the liberty of a boy and say that he must stay on the farm, but the people who are coming to this country should be induced to go on the land. The farmer may be a sinner in some respects; he must give his hired man a home and if the hired man wants to marry and raise a family he should be allowed to do so. If this principle is carried out we

will solve the question of agricultural production and of the high cost of living all over the country. There is no other legitimate way to do it. If we get down to the common sense of these things we must let the man who comes in from Europe or anywhere else feel that he is a part and parcel of the state, he should enter into our social conditions, be associated with our churches and schools and in this way become a living factor and a useful citizen in the neighbourhood in which he lives.
Then, we had a speech from our hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark). They had him at school but he has not improved any. They sent him down to Nova Scotia and they put him up against those big industries to see if they could break up that Cobden platform of his, but he came back as bad as ever. The hon. gentleman who took him down there is not in his seat just now, but I would say: Do not give up hope; there is hope as long as there is life. Take him down again. I was very much pleased to see and to hear that there was some possibility of amendment. The hon. member for Red Deer never seriously moved against the tariff while his own friends were in power although he is finding fault with that tariff to-day. I do not know that he has ever moved a resolution upon the subject. It is a strange thing that hon. gentlemen opposite now want profane hands to be laid upon that sacred edifice that they built. It was the greatest thing that ever happened in this country, it gave us all this enormous prosperity and now they want the thing torn down. They want profane hands to be laid upon it. The only thing that has been done with it so far is that it has been cut down a little but they are finding fault with it still. They thought it was a blessing five years ago, three years ago, eight years ago; it is a question whether it should not still be considered a blessing. That it may be improved we all know, but the last people who should find fault with it are the men who designed it and put it upon the statute book. But I suppose they must say something to the people and in a few years they will say it is a Tory tariff, that the Tories made it. That is what is going to happen. I will tell hon. gentlemen opposite that there is no doubt it will be improved and improved in the interests of this country. It is quite right that any tariff should have a certain degree of permanence about it, but conditions change and the tariff must change to suit the conditions. I am willing to go that far and to toll my right 12i
hon. friend that I have not the slightest doubt that it will be properly dealt with when the proper time comes.
There has been a good deal said about free wheat. I am not going to say much about that question because I cannot discuss it from the viewpoint of the western man, but I desire to say that the future of our western country is largely bound up in the fact that they must enter upon mixed farming. If they enter upon mixed farming they will get the bi-product of the wheat and the bi-product of the wheat is a very important factor in mixed farming. It is the life-blood of the dairy industry of Ontario and Quebec to-day. It is of the utmost importance that we should see to it that we have our wheat ground within this country and the flour exported to England or to any other country, because if the bi-product of the wheat is transferred to England or to some other country the dairy industry suffers very materially as a result. This bi-product can be shipped on the wheat at a less freight cost than it can after it is ground; hence the necessity of grinding the wheat in this country. Instead of being able to grind wheat into flour for about 14,000,000 people we should be able to grind for 50,000,000 people. How is it that with wheat shipped from Manitoba to Ontario, the millers can sell the flour cheaper to the Ontario man than to the man in Manitoba-simply because the bi-product has to be shipped out of Manitoba at a very heavy freight rate. This bi-product is virtually the profit of the miller and it is cheaper to ship the wheat down here, grind and sell the bran and shorts than to grind the wheat into flour in Manitoba and to ship the biproducts down here in bulk.
The men who look upon this question from the mere advantage of a few months hence are not perhaps looking at it from the proper standpoint of the future of this country. It is a good thing to see our western provinces taking up the question of raising milch cows and going into dairy products. We should have enough of these products to satisfy our own people.
