1,000	lbs. per cow more than it was ten years previously. But that does not justify the falling off in the number of our cattle, because if we had the same number of cows in the older provinces in 1911 as we had in 1901, our product would be equal to

the domestic consumption, and we would be exporting as well. The serious thing is that we 'are exporting no butter and we have lost our place altogether in the British market for that commodity. A few years ago I was bold enough to make the statement in this House that in the near future Russian Siberia would be a serious rival to us in many of the important products of our farm, and at the time my Liberal friends ridiculed the idea of Russia interfering with our market in England. But what is the fact to-day? Russian Siberia is second of all the countries of the world in the quantity of butter she ships to the English markets; Denmark is first. We have lost our butter trade there, and it is taken by others, and it will not be an easy matter to regain our position. Now there is another important consideration that I wish to point out, and that is that if the other counties in Ontario equalled in the number of cattle and the dairy output a few counties in Ontario, some in eastern Ontario and one or two in western Ontario, we would have double the number of cattle we have in the entire province at the present time. This shows the possibilities before the people of this country if they conscientiously enter upon the problem of knowing what an acre of land is worth. If it be possible, the Government should endeavour to show the people of Canada the possibilities of 100 acres of land. The boy or the man who goes into a corn field and sees but the weeds and the corn, is living far short of his privilege; he should see nature unfolding her designs to feed the world. That is his business. He should feel he is a factor in doing so, and if he does not

realize it, he is falling far short of his duty. Supposing this country were a finished country as some. countries of Europe are, what would it mean to the world? Canada would be standing in the gateways of the world, holding out food to the hungry, so to speak; taking her great share in supplying the food of the world and doing her duty as an agricultural country. We are this year exporting enormously over what we were exporting last year. I have a little clipping here from the Star, and it quotes from the report of the United States Department of Agriculture Report, and it says this:
Canada is tha largest purchaser of American automobiles according to figures compiled by the United States Department of Commerce. The Dominion took 5,824 automobiles from the United States in the first eleven months of 1913, valued at $7,870,000.
We can not be very hard up when we can do that; we bought nearly $8,000,000 worth of automobiles from the United States in the eleven months, to say nothing about those made in Canada. I believe the farmer should have an automobile; no man in the world deserves it better than he if he can afford it, but when he is able to buy automobiles at this rate, he cannot be so terribly straitened in circumstances. I read further:
During the month of December, according to figures issued by the Department of Customs, the exports of Canada underwent a remarkable increase. The export of domestic produce during December 1913 amounted to $55,803,642, as against $38,658,625 in December 1912, the increase thus being $17,145,017 or 44%. By far the largest item in the total was the export of agricultural products which stood at $35,367,942 as against $22,859,325-
This would seem to back up my statement that the farmers are well off,- at least in Ontario.
-which stood at $35,367,942 as against $22,859,325 in the corresponding month of 1912, the increase being a trifle over $12,800,000 or nearly 55%. There also was a heavy proportionate increase in the export of manufactures, the figures being $5,599,086 as against $3,800,805, the increase being within a few dollars of $1,800,000 or more than 47%.
This does not prove there are so many unemployed.
There was also a heavy increase in export of animals and their products, the figures standing at $4,744,056 as against $2,791,550, the increase being $1,952,506 or nearly 70 per cent.
That no doubt is accounted for to a large extent by the shipments of cattle from this country to the United States. Taking the nine months, however, in which these shipments did not occur, there is still a large increase.
During the nine months' period ending December 31, 1913, the exports coming under the head of agriculture showed an increase of about 50 per cent over those of the corresponding period of 1912. They stood at $177,706,169 as against $119,209,170 in the earlier period, the increase being $58,696,999 in the nine months.
That does not look as if there were very hard times.
Animals and their produce also showed a substantial increase, from $36,740,883 to $43,568,859.
That shows an increase during the' nine months when .there were no shipments of cattle from Canada to the United States, owing to the fact that such shipments could not be made until the tariff was changed.	.
In regard to the products of the fisheries, the imports alone have fallen off to some extent during that period, no doubt because merchants were cautious as to buying owing to the talk of stringent times throughout the country.
I think, Mr. Speaker, u would be permissible for me to tell a story that was told the other day in the American Senate, because our friends here, who are so fond of reciprocity, would surely let me reciprocate in this respect. Our friends on the opposite side of the House are looking all the time for calamities, financial crises and financial panics.' The leader of the Republican party in the American Senate is like my right hon. friend, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, in that respect. The leader of the Democratic side of the House told this story. He said that a man with an eye out came along one day to the doctor. The man said, ' Doctor, I want an eye put in. I don't want no glass eye; I want a flesh eye, one I can see with.' The doctor said, 'All right, I can put in a cat's eye.' The man said, ' All right, go ahead;' so the doctor fixed the man up. Some time later when the doctor saw the man again, he said, ' How are you getting along?' ' Oh,' the man says, * all right, but that eternal thing is looking for rats and mice all the time. Our friends are looking for rats and mice all the time. Of course, they are not going to find them, but I shall leave them in that position when I take my seat.

I have followed with great interest and great pleasure indeed the very witty speech which has just been delivered by my genial friend the hon. member for Dundas (Mr. Broder). After having listened to him last

summer in his own good constituency, where I noticed that he was friendly with Tories and Grits alike, and that he could tell a good story to both and thus be elected
by large majorities, I can only repeat what I then said, namely, that the hon. gentleman should be transferred to another chamber. He has deserved that from his party for the many services which he has rendered the cause in the many townships and back concessions of Ontario, where he has been able to roll up the Tory majorities by his witty stories. There is a vacancy at present, and, speaking in all frankness, I am quite sure that the farmers of the province of Ontario, the farmers of Canada generally, would be proud to see my genial friend in the Senate.
In regard to the Speech from the Throne, I can only re-echo what has been said on all sides of this House, that the people in Canada, and I might say in particular the people of the province of Quebec, whose reverence for the Royal Family is well known, were most happy to learn that Her Royal Highness had so speedily recovered.
I have listened with great pleasure to the speech delivered by the new member for the county of York, N.B. (Mr. McLeod), and I must compliment him upon the very good impression he has made on the members of this House. He succeeds a member who for many years sat with us, and played quite a part in the debates of Parliament; I refer to Mr. Crocket, now Mr. Justice Crocket. By, the way, I see that my good friend the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) is in his seat. Would he explain to the House how it is that under his benevolent eye appointments to the judiciary are made from the House of Commons, when some years ago the voice of my hon. friend rang in tones of indignation against the appointments made by the right hon. the leader of the late Government (Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier), because, forsooth, he appointed members of the House to the judiciary? My hon. friend from York has been elected to this House by acclamation, and I congratulate him upon this; but he has come through one of the broken pledges of the right hon. the leader of the Government and the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce, namely, that no appointments should be made from members of the House of Commons. The hon. member for York, his countenance beaming with optimism, told us that this country was but slightly touched by a wave of adversity. In New Brunswick, he said, money had never been so easy as it was last year. I wonder what is the opinion

of my good friend from Carleton, N.B., about the easy money in New Brunswick.
Not so easy now as it was two years ago.

I was surprised when my hon. friend from York made that statement. Oh, blessed Arcadia! Who owns the magic wand by which money is made so easy in New Brunswick and so stringent in poor Quebec and poor Ontario?
I have listened also with interest to the speech delivered by my hon. friend from Bellechasse (Mr. Lavallee). He spoke with eloquence, and I hope that some day he will repeat in the English language what he said so well in his own mother tongue. Evidently the hon. member for Bellechasse has seen the light. I have known his parentage in the province of Quebec. He comes from good old Liberal stock, and I noticed that when he spoke the other day there was quite a tremor in his voice. He had evidently filled a gap, because, if I mistake not, at the last general election in the county of Bellechasse he ran, not as a Conservative, but as a Nationalist. Evidently, as we say in French ' II y a fagots et fagots '-there are Nationalists and Nationalists. Listening to the speeches of my hon. friend I find it departs from the red hot Nationalism to deep azure blue Toryism. ' II y a fagots et fagots '-there are Nationalists and Nationalists. He may claim to be still a Nationalist; but I say that he belongs to the insincere school of Nationalists. For there are a few sincere Nationalists in this country to-day-oh, very, very few indeed! I would like to know what his leader of yesterday, Mr. Bourassa, thinks of his opinions to-day. I am sure that if Mr. Bourassa were to write to the hon. member for Bellechasse he could not sign his letter as of yore with the subscription 'Yours sincerely.' But then, my hon. friend in his new Tory venture, has outrun himself, it seems to me. He has evidently delivered himself to my hon. friend the Postmaster General, who listened, yes, listened attentively to his enlogy. In his new zeal, the member for Bellechasse went so far as to compare the present Postmaster General with Sir George Etienne Cartier. Yes, he said that the present Postmaster General is the political heir of the great Conservative chieftain. If it were mine to give advice to my hon. friend from Bellechasse, I would give him the advice given by Talleyrand, the master of cynics and diplomats, to a young undersecretary who intended to enter the career

of diplomacy. He came to Talleyrand for counsel and Talleyrand said to him ' Et surtout pas de zele! '-above all, no zeal! This is the advice I would give to my hon. friend when he compares his new leader, the Nationalist of yesterday and the Tory of to-day with Sir George Etienne Cartier.
Now, coming to the Speech from the Throne, if I consider it in the constitutional light, I see it as a lever to put the parliamentary machinery in motion. The Speech from the Throne has to be delivered annually, just as a certain Chinese daily gazette which was published under the Ming dynasty had to be issued, with or without news. One day the newspaper appeared blank. The editor was asked: 'But why do you publish your paper-there is no news in it, there are no articles in it? ' He answered:	' But it has to be
issued; it is a daily gazette.' So with tne Speech from the Throne: it has to be delivered, it is the lever which puts the parliamentary machinery in motion. But, Sir, that speech is a blank; it is barren of any legislative proposals; it bears the evidence of hard times, notwithstanding my hon. friend from Dundas (Mr. Broder). It is as meagre as Canada's last Christmas dinner; it is as empty as the workingman's pail; it is as bare as a church plate at times; it is as nude as the spite wall on Elgin street. Its nudity borders on indecency.
But, before going into the few announcements which the speech contains, let me, for a moment, take a glance at it. First of all, I see that there is general satisfaction expressed at the fact that there has been a great expansion of trade. Indeed, we all know that, since 1897, there has been a tremendous expansion of trade. And my hon. friend the leader of the Government stated the other day that the expansion of trade which began in 1897 was not due to the fiscal policy of the leader of the Opposition, but that it was due to the old National Policy, and that the Liberal party on assuming office, had not altered that policy by one jot or tittle-that it had remained unchanged and that indeed the country had prospered notwithstanding the Liberal party. May I read the speech, or part of it, which was delivered by the old stalwart, the veteran of the Conservative party, Sir Charles Tupper-and we rejoice to know that he still enjoys perfect health-on the morrow of the introduction in this House in 1897 of the British preference, a policy coupled with the tariff resolutions introduced by the then Minister of Finance, Hon. Mr. Fielding?
We all remember that Sir Charles Tupper, speaking from the seat now adorned by the present leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), prophesied that the manufacturers in the various industries of this country would suffer, and suffer lamentably, if the Liberal policy propounded by Mr. Fielding were maintained. He said:
The result is that this tariff goes into operation and the hon. gentleman knows that the industries of this country are already paralyzed in consequence, while hon. members gloat over the destruction of Canadian industries. I was reading the wail, the sorrowful wail, of these industries in the Montreal Gazette, where one manufacturer after another declared that those industries were ruined, that their mills must close, and that they saw staring them in the face a return to the deplorable state of things that existed when the hon. gentlemall who last addressed the House was in charge of the fiscal policy of this country. I say that a deeper wrong was never inflicted upon Canada.
I feel that so far from rejoicing at it from a party standpoint, I deplore from the bottom of my heart the ruin that is going to be inflicted upon the best interests of Canada, and upon its great industries. Still, I unhesitatingly say that, from a party point of view, the hon. gentlemen are doing our work; they are showing the people of this country that no reliance can be placed upon the most solemn declarations that they make either in the House or out of it; they are showing the people of this country that, having obtained power, which was all they wished for, they are now prepared to abuse that power at a cost of sacrifice of the industries of Canada.
I am glad to say that the sad predictions of ibis great veteran were not fulfilled. Under the fiscal policy of the Hon. Mr. Fielding, coupled with the British preference, with the abolition of all the specific duties and the altering the duties on two hundred and fifty-five items of the Budget, I am glad to say, the country has prospered and expanded.
But we were told something else in 1911. We were warned that our trade should not be fostered with our big neighbour, the United States, that we should instead cultivate an interprovincial trade, and that we should maintain our connection with the mother country by still increasing our trade with Great Britain. Mr. Speaker, not later than the month of May last, I had the privilege of being present at a dinner given by the Government of Canada to the American bankers then visiting the city of Ottawa. Will you listen to the language of Mr. James J. Hill, a gentleman born in Canada, who has become in the United States a great railway magnate, as we know. Speaking about the trade relations between Canada and the United States, Mr. Hill

made the following statement in the presence of the Minister 'of Finance and of the Prime Minister of Canada:
Most countries have been accustomed to value their relations with one another by the total money value of the commerce between them; and, rightly or wrongly, they have laid special stress upon that difference between imports and exports which is known as the balance of trade. Without asserting any theory as to its value as an indicator of prosperity or the contrary, both of which views have ardent champions, both sides will agree upon the fact that it is an important measure of commercial intercourse. In spite of all obstructions the commercial relations between Canada and the United States have grown to proportions that astonish even those familiar with the official figures. According to the report of the United States consul in this city, the foreign trade of Canada reached a total of over a billion dollars for the calendar year 1912. The increase over 1911 was 23.5 per cent. Of the total, 56 per cent was business done with the United States. For that same calendar year the balance of trade for the whole United States was $581,000,000 ; and of this $255,000,000 was due to our commerce with Canada. It supplied 44 per cent of the balance rolled up by our commerce with the whole world.
It is usual to speak and think of Europe as the best customer of the United States; and in so far as this refers to the United Kingdom, it is true. But the Dominion of Canada is far and away the second-best customer we have. The statistics have been brought down to cover the first ten months of the current fiscal year, which began on the first day of last July. During that time our exports to the United Kingdom were $524,000,000 ; to Germany, $291,000,000 ; to France, $131,000,000 ; to Canada, $338,000,000, and to all Europe combined, $1,294,000,000. No other country except Great [DOT] Britain and Germany even approaches Canada-aJs a buyer in the markets of the United States.
Mr. Hill talks common sense; he does not mix up loyalty with business.
This business has been done not by reason of any sentiment whatever about it on the part of either country, or of any artificial favouring conditions, but simply because it is more profitable for both to deal with each other than for either to deal anywhere else in a large percentage of its commercial transactions. And nothing can reverse or annul that condition which nature herself has established.
Further on, Mr. Hill compares the trade of Canada with the total trade between the United States and Seuth America. He concludes thus:
Swing the net still wider, and take in both American continents, from the Arctic Circle on the north to Cape Horn on the south, add Cuba and all the West Indies by whomsoever controlled, that nothing between the two oceans may escape. We did, in these ten months, a total export business of $630,000,000 with this western hemisphere; and of the whole Canada furnished fifty-four per cent. It seems to me that a connection so immense and so valuable to both parties is the central and controlling 
fact of every occasion like the present, when business men from both sides of the line get together to take stock of their present and their future.
At six o'clock the House took re-cess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

Just before recess, Mr. Speaker, I was quoting a few sentences from a very elaborate address delivered in the city of Ottawa by that great Canadian, James J. Hill. This speech of Mr. Hill's, telling of the immense expansion of trade between Canada, our country, and the great republic to the south of us-and especially during the two years of the present Administration-only shows this cold fact: that you Cannot legislate against geography, and it furnishes the best rejoinder to that nonsensical slogan of the last general election, * No truck and no trade with the United States of America.' As I stated a moment ago, there are many things which should appear in the Speech from the Throne but which are not to be found in it. I have been reared in a school which, for many years, taught that there was no possibility of establishing a mutual preference between the mother country and Canada, but dnr-ing the fifteen years that our hon. friends opposite were sitting on this side of the House, we were repeatedly told that as soon as the Conservatives came into office, steps would be taken to have that famous mutual preference established between Canada and Great Britain. I did not expect that the right hon. gentleman the leader of the Government would implement the promises of his party at the first session of this Parliament. We gave him time. The second session came, but not a word about mutual preference. Oh, Mr. Speaker, I have a vague suspicion that the centralization policy advocated last year so earnestly by Mr. Bonar Law on the one hand, and by Mr. Churchill on the other, was perhaps the first step towards mutual preference. At all events nothing came out of it. But now in this third session of the Conservative Administration, when things have found their level and when the Conservative party is in a position to accomplish something, we find nothing in the Speech from the Throne to indicate that steps will be taken at the earliest oppertunity to establish mutual preference in trade matters between the mother country and Canada. I for one, do not believe in that policy. I think that if mutual preference were established, far from uniting the Dominions to the mother country, it would

estrange them. And further, in my humble judgment, it would estrange Great Britain on fiscal lines from the other countries of the world. But it is the policy of the Tory party in England, or at least the policy of one section of it, and it has been the policy preached by one large section of the Imperialist party of Canada. I do not argue that the Government should implement its promise in that regard. In my humble judgment such a policy would not be advantageous. I believe in the close relations of the mother country with Canada, but not on such a basis. * History,' to quote Webster, ' is not only the record of events; it is also the record of human experience.' In days of yore there was a preference between the mother country and the colonies. Every student of Canadian history will remember that before the repeal of the Corn Laws there was a British preference for colonial products, for Canadian products. But when, under the leadership of the two greatest men of the last century, Richard Cobden and John Bright, England espoused the cause of free trade, and when Sir Robert Peel, the Conservative Premier, repealed the Corn Laws, the British preference was abolished. What was the result as regards Canada? As soon as that preference was repealed there was discontent, there was rancour, there was bitterness and soreness of heart, and the first thing our political ancestors heard of was the famous annexation manifesto. The repeal of the British preference in favour of Canadian products was the cause of the issuance of the annexation manifesto of 1849. At the last general election I heard some of my hon. friends opposite repeating again that old story, that the reciprocity programme of the Liberal party would bring about the annexation of Canada to the United States. Some people had enough brass to repeat such a fairy tale. What was the cure of the annexation spirit which manifested itself in 1849? What, were the words of wisdom spoken by that great Governor General Lord Elgin (the scion of a great Tory family) in 1849, after the repeal of the British preference and the announcement of the annexation proclivities of Canada? Listen to this language. Surely it is applicable to-day. On November 8, 1849, in a letter to Earl Grey, the ancestor of our late Governor General, Lord Elgin wrote as follows:
So long as this state of things continues there will be discontent in this country; deep growing discontent. You will not, I trust, accuse me of having deceived you on this point. I have always said that I am prepared to assume the
responsibility of keeping Canada quiet, with a much smaller garrison than we have now, and without .any tax on the British consumer in the shape of protection to Canadian products, if you put our trade on as good a footing as that of our American neighbours; but if things remain on their present footing in this respect, there is nothing before us but violent agitation, ending in convulsion or annexation.
History repeating itself! Oh, certainly, Mr. Speaker, we do not expect to hear of any annexation movement in Canada just now. We are not now in the midst of a general election, so we may all proclaim our faith in British citizenship and in Canadian citizenship. There will never be any question as regards the deep and intense loyalty of every Canadian, whatever may be his faith on fiscal matters, bi$t there will be agitation in this country, and very serious agitation, particularly on the western prairies, as long as the present serious discontent exists.
Sir, the Government takes credit in the fact that the moving of the crops from the western prairies to the seaboard has been made easy and smooth. The Government thinks that our transportation facilities are adequate. Sir, I take that as the greatest compliment to the policy of the Liberal party during the last sixteen years in which they held office. My hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) and my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) know that ten years ago, eight years ago, seven years ago, at the fall of every year, there was the fear that there would be a car shortage at the head of the Great Lakes. There is no more dread of a car shortage and I wish to pay here my compliments to the three great transcontinental railways of Canada. The Liberal party are not responsible for the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway system, but as my hon. friend from Edmonton pointed out the other evening, the double tracking of the Canadian Pacific railway was the direct consequence of the transportation policy of the Liberal party whilst in office. They are responsible for the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway without the degrading of the same line. The statement was made, by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. White) that the Liberal party was primarily responsible for the construction of the Canadian Northern system. We know, and I am in the judgment of my friends who represent the Great Lakes districts in this House, that the harbours of the Great Lakes have been improved by the immediate predecessors of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works. The St. Lawrence channel system was rushed to completion from 1896 until 1910. It was made

free from tolls by the Liberal party which was a bold policy, but the Liberal party did it. The ship channel between Montreal and Quebec was deepened; the port of Montreal was equipped as no other on the North American continent; and the port of Quebec was also equipped. I am glad to hear that the Government are going to complete that equipment. I hope that my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) is in earnest in the promises he has made to his Quebec supporters that the equipment of the port of Montreal will be completed.
Speaking of transportation, Mr. Speaker, I am surprised, after the many speeches that have been delivered especially around Montreal by hon. gentlemen of the Conservative party, some of whom I see before me now, to find nothing in the Speech from the Throne about the Georgian Bay canal. I am in favour of the Georgian bay canal, but if I mistake not, the moneys which were voted last year will be spent for just one link of that great international route. I believe that the Georgian Bay canal will be completed as soon as the improvement reaches a certain point on lake Nipissing. I hope I may be wrong, but, Sir, I am told by many that it is not the intention of the Government, in view of the intense rivalry existing between southern Ontario and northern Ontario, to proceed any further than lake Nipissing with the Georgian Bay canal.
While speaking about transportation, my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) was taken to task after prorogation, because, forsooth, he had not found it possible to settle the vexed question of ocean rates. Articles were published in the Tory press, and a statement was delivered even by the talented young man who is now Chairman of the Railway Commission, that with regard to this question of ocean freight rates the guilty man was my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals. Well, the Chairman of the Railway Commission has gone to England. He has interviewed the mighties in England, the heads of the great navigation companies, and he has returned to Canada. What success has he obtained? What work has he accomplished? If he had accomplished something, if he had achieved any success, surely mention would be made of it in the Speech from the Throne.
We are informed that there will be a Civil Service Bill. I am told-I may be mistaken-perhaps my hon. friend may correct me-that it has already been distributed; but, if so, it has not been my good fortune to read it, At all events, it is the 
beginning, I suppose, of that much desired and much talked of civil service reform. Is it, Mr. Speaker, to be based on Sir George Murray's report? Are we going to have an army of under-secretaries? I know that many of the young talented bloods of the Conservative party have been promised under-secretaryships. Perhaps it explains why some amongst my hon. friends of the Nationalist party have become rabid zealots of the Tory party. Are we going to have under-secretaries, or is the Conservative party going to improve, if it can be improved, the Civil Service Act introduced by the ex-Minister of Agriculture-I refer to the Hon. Sydney Fisher? We may differ as to Mr. Fisher's politics. I regard him as one of the ablest men who ever sat in this Parliament, and, with all due respect to my hon. friend from Chateauguay (Mr. Morris), the new member whom I am pleased to see seated here this evening, I think that the loss of Chateauguay was Canada's loss, that the defeat of Mr. Fisher was the defeat of the House of Commons and of Canada. Mr. Fisher was the first one to introduce a real Civil Service Bill based on the competitive system; that is to say, the British system.
It is universally admitted, that whether he serves at home, or in the Crown colonies, or in the Indian Empire, the British civil servant is the most efficient in the world. And, Sir, that is because the spoils system is unknown in England and because the man who enters the British civil service knows that he has a career in that service. But the great Conservative party in this country, always so ready to speak ill of American politics, has since it came to power applied to the Canadian Civil Service the worst feature of American politics, namely, the spoils system. The Liberal party, following the lead of the Hon. Mr. Fisher, adopted the first Civil Service Bill based jon competitive examinations for the inside service, and although I have asked the Postmaster General for the last two years if he intended to apply that beneficent system to the thousands of employees in the outside service of the post office, I have been able to elicit from him only smiles and vague answers. I trust that the Civil Service Bill which is promised in the Speech from the Throne, will extend to the outside civil service of Canada, the protection and benefits now conferred on the inside service.
We are informed in the speech that at last a Redistribution Bill will be introduc-

ed this session. There are not many members in this House to-day-there are none with the exception of the right hon. the leader of the Opposition and yourself, Mr. Speaker-who were present in 1882 when the first Redistribution Bill was introduced by Sir John A. Macdonald's Government. But, though we were not present we all know what scars the gerrymander of 1882 left on the hearts of the Liberal electors of Ontario. We know that in 1882 and again in 1892 an attempt was made, to use an old Tory expression:	to dish the
Grits, and we know that by picking out a township here and a township there, the Tory gerrymander created a few Grit hives to serve the purposes of the Tory party. But, Sir, what was done in 1882, and what was perpetrated in spite of Liberal protests in 1892, is no longer possible in this year of 1914. Let us not forget what the Hon. Edward Blake suggested to Sir John A. Macdonald. He told him that although he could not successfully prevail against the advantage he had to carve the constituencies as it suited him, yet he should at least respect the historic boundaries of Ontario and Quebec. In 1902, when in turn it fell to the lot of the Liberal party to introduce a Redistribution Bill, what was the policy pursued by the right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, then Prime Minister? Some young Liberals of that day, animated with an undue party spirit, expected that the Conservatives then sitting in opposition would get a dose of the same medicine they had served out to the Liberals in 1882 and 1892. But, the great leader of the Liberal party, always fair, then gave a lesson not only to his opponents but to the too fervid partisans of his own party, and he introduced a Bill with a schedule in blank, leaving it to a joint committee of the House to delimit the constituencies. And, on the report of that joint committee the Bill was introduced, which, as you well know, Mr. Speaker, was never criticised and was adopted unanimously. That was the Liberal method in 1902 as contrasted with the Tory method in 1882 and 1892.
Was the report submitted by the committee concurred in by all its members?

The question is a fair one and I shall answer it. As I remember, when the Bill, based on the report of the Committee, was introduced, it was suggested that the two ridings of Hastings had been improperly dealt with and that they should be divided differently, and Sir Wilfrid Laurier acceded to that request and the Bill
was amended in that respect and made unanimous.
The hon. member is mistaken.

I shall be glad to hear the hon. gentleman correct me if he can, but I appeal to his spirit of fair play, and I ask if it is not a fact that the Redistribution Bill of 1902 was considered, even by the opponents of the Liberal party, as a fair measure giving justice to Liberals and to Conservatives alike. With my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark), I do trust in the spirit of fair play and the sense of honour of the right hon. the Prime Minister of Canada. Why should we not rely on the honour of the Prime Minister of Canada, and who will believe for a moment that he would descend to mean tactics to dish a political opponent? I do not believe that the Prime Minister of Canada would descend to dishing the Grits, and neither do I believe that public opinion would stand for it in this year of grace 1914.
I am told, I may be wrong, and I shall be glad to be corrected if I am wrong, that there are sinister influences behind the Prime Minister of Canada. I am told, for instance, that my hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames), whom I regret not to see in his seat and my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) have been consulting their friends around the country in the province of Quebec, to know whether this or that parish, this or that ward on the island of Montreal, should not be better annexed to this or that county. I am not positive about it. It is rumoured, and if it is not true I would be only too glad that it is not.
A Bill will also be introduced to increase the representation in the Upper House. The notice is already on the notice paper. Do you not think, Mr. Speaker, that in this connection there is an undue haste to pour new blood into the august chamber? Where is my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster)? Why, to increase the representation in the Senate Chamber, to think of reforming the Senate by deforming it! Where is the hon. member for Lincoln? Mr. Speaker, do you remember his speeches against the Senate? His silence at the present time, to say the least, is very ominous. I was reading the other day the memoirs of a woman of genius, Madame de Stael. In the preface of that work, I came across a sentence. Madame de Stael had been expelled from France by orders of the Emperor Napoleon; she was sojourning in Germany and was writing to a

friend. She said, ' Since Bonaparte lias been crowned Emperor of France, a great silence has been heard in Europe.' I found the expression ' to hear a silence ' rather strange. It must indeed be a very ominous silence. Sir, I hear the silence of my hon. friend from Lincoln when mention is made of an increase in the number of the Senators. Is he dreaming, perad-venture, of a Senatorship or is he sleeping on the woolsack expectations?
This is briefly the bill of fare for this year. There are several courses of platitudes for the party heelers, but there is a diet of negations for the Canadian people. There is nothing about the economic conditions of the country. What is the chief topic to-day in the cities, in the rural parts of Canada, in the homes of Canada? The high cost of living, the fiscal revolution created by the unemployment of the labouring masses and the agitation in the West for free wheat. The Government answers with words to the clamours of the people. My hon. friend the Minister of Play-he describes himself as the Minister of Play, and I hope I am not libelling him when referring in this way to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers)- was asked the other day his opinion about the present high cost of living. What was his answer given at Halifax, the capital of Nova Scotia, represented by the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Borden) and by that able gentleman the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean)? Oh, he offered a cure to the ills of the high cost of living. Here is what he said:
To my mind the high cost of living is an indication of the prosperity and expansion of the country. If you want cheap living, give us a few years of hard times.
This is what fell from the lips of my hon. friend the Minister of Labour. There are more than words in this answer. It is adding insult to irony. It reminds me of what happened three or four years ago when the Clemenceau Government was defeated in the French Parliament. It was after a speech delivered by the Prime Minister, by that old tiger, Mr. Clemenceau, who had made quite a witty speech; but his speech was in a way rather unfortunate, and as a result a vote was taken and the Government was defeated. Some one went to that caustic journalist, Henri Rochefort, to get his opinion about the fall of the Government. Mr. Rochefort's quick retort was, ' The Government has committed suicide by firing words into its brain.' When I read the 
answer given by the hon. Minister of Labour, that hard times are a good thing for the country, I say that the Government is committing suicide by firing words into its brain.
Sir, what is the situation to-day after two years of Conservative rule in Canada? It is admitted that when the Liberal party left office three years ago we had enjoyed fifteen years of abundant prosperity, so much so that, when the elections of 1911 took place, our friends on the other side traversed the country and preached to the people of Canada the wholesome gospel of ' let well enough alone.' The trade of Canada was buoyant and our credit in the financial world was excellent. Canada's loans were at that time considered as the leading and best securities on the London financial market. What is the situation today? Is it not a fact that we are facing a most terrible industrial unrest in this country in spite of the high protection which the manufacturers of Canada are enjoying? Who on the other 3ide of the House speaks of the strike at Nanaimo where Canadians were ordered to shoot on Canadians? Do you remember, Mr. Speaker, the speech delivered by the hon. Minister of Militia (Mr. Hughes) two years ago when he said:

They were ordered to fire on the strikers of Nanaimo. Many of the strikers are in jail to-day. Let us come now to Vancouver. I am informed that in Vancouver there are 17,000 people out of employment. Let us come to Regina. There the mounted police are obliged at this moment to put down bread riots. Think of it; in the great wheatgrowing district of Regina we actually have bread riots and the mounted police are obliged to protect citizens against the rioters.

Will the hon. gentleman permit me a question? Will he kindly inform the House the authority for his statement that there are 17,000 out of work in Vancouver? And will he permit me to make a very brief statement?

So much the better for Vancouver. My information is to the contrary. That, however, is a matter that can be ascertained. The Board of Trade and the Relief Organization, the Mayor and councillors-the powers that be in Vancouver-are investigating the question. Two thousand five hundred-it is not difficult to investigate that number. . I suspect there is a little more * than that. At all events, I take the word of my hon. friend. We shall get the facts, I am quite sure, after the investigation by the Relief Committee, the Mayor and other authorities.
Will the hon. gentleman tell us when the bread riot occurred in Regina?
I read it in the press only a few days ago.
It was only a joke.

No joke in that. It has not been contradicted in the press. We have the members from the West on this side of the House, and I am assured that the mounted police have been ordered to patrol the streets of Regina in order to prevent a riot.
I was in Regina myself on the night to which the press refers, and I can assure the hon. gentleman that there was no bread riot or any other riot.

In Winnipeg we have, according to the Mayor, three thousand men unemployed. In Toronto, I suppose, everybody is working? But I happened to be in the city of Toronto on the 12th of the present month. It was the day of the inaugural address delivered by Mayor Hocken. If my hon. friend will take the trouble-for me it is always a pleasure -to read the Toronto News of the 12th instant, he will see a big headline, something like the great ' scare heads ' that we had in the last election, showing that Mayor Hocken said: Before proceeding to business, gentlemen who have been newly elected, we must proceed to the relief of the 15,000 people who are out of employment in the city of Toronto. Now, in Montreal, whither I go occasionally-Montreal, which is represented by my hon. friend from Maison-neuve (Mr. Verville)-there are 40,000 people out of employment. I know as a matter of fact that the hours of labour have been reduced in the Angus shops, in the Grand Trunk shops, in the Canada Car shops. I will not name other shops where the people are simply put out of employment for the whole winter. In Quebec-I appeal to my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) as to this-were it not for the Government works this winter there would be serious trouble in that city. Is it not a fact that the principal trade of Quebec, the shoe trade, is now locked up ? Is it not a fact that we have had strikes and lockouts all along the Intercolonial railway from the city of Levis to the city of Halifax? Last year the Government boasted of the prosperity of the country. This year, unfortunately, we are the sad witnesses of a declining trade, a shrinking revenue, and unemployment. And the excuse given by the Minister of Finance for this sad condition of things is: Oh, well, in 1907-08 there was also a temporary check. Yes, it is true, in 1907-08 there was a temporary check in the prosperity of the country. But concurrently with that temporary check there was a cut in the expenditure of the Dominion. Under the Liberal Government, in the last year that Government was in office, the expenditure amounted to $120,000,000. This year, in the day of adversity, the national expenditure amounts to $250,000,000 in round figures.
The credit of Canada in the financial world has been impaired, I do not wish to be unduly severe with the Minister of Finance; I have a good deal of sympathy for him. If he were now in his seat I would ask him permission to say that he may well raise his standard and his ideals to the height of the standard and ideals of Hon. W. S. Fielding, his predecessor as Minister of Finance. With Mr. Fielding, statesmanship was more than empty words; it was character, it was conviction; it was sincerity of purpose; it was service and fitness. I say again, the Minister of Finance may well look up to his predecessor as an exemplar.
The Minister of Finance complains that the Liberal London press has been inspired -as if the London Tory press last year during our debate on the $35,000,000 tribute had not been daily inspired from this country representing the Liberal party as a party of disloyal men. Leaving aside the London Chronicle, which, according to its standard of ethics does not publish anything except the truth about our financial condition, let us take the Pall Mall Gazette,

a Tory paper in London which shrieks its jingoism daily. What did the Pall Mall Gazette say about the last loan venture of the Minister of Finance? It said that it was the greatest fiasco which ever took place in England in the case of a Canadian loan. What about the Daily Mail, a paper with a large circulation, devoted to the jingo party in London? The Daily Mail on December 16 used the following language:
Canadians, until recently, stood easily highest
amongst the Colonial securities and not many months ago the Dominion of Canada's 35 per cents (there was no 4 per cent then) stood some half a dozen points higher than corresponding western Australian stock, whereas now, the western Australian 4 per cents recently issued at 97 stand at 2 premium, while Canadian 4 per cents issued at the same price stand at one-half discount.
Sir, the financial stringency of 1907 affected the whole financial world, but during that period Canada, under the financial leadership of Mr. Fielding, the ex-Minister of Finance, was never branded as it was of late by the jingo Tory press of Lon-dofi, England. Sir, Mr. Fielding preserved the credit of Canada not only at home but abroad during the stress of 1911.
I now come to that vexed question of the high cost of living. In Canada, a young country rich in resources, it is abnormal that during the last ten years the percentage of increase in the cost of living has reached the figure of 57 per cent, as against 15 per cent in Great Britain and 17 per cent in the United States. I know that the causes of the high cost of living are many and diverse. I know that we can attribute this condition partly to depreciation in the value of gold, partly to the desertion of land, to the increased urban population, to uneconomic methods of marketing, to a wrong system of cold storage, and to the trusts and mergers. Speaking about cold storage, I observe that my genial friend across the way (Mr. Bradbury) has a Bill on the Order Paper to regulate the cold storage trusts. I hope this Bill will be taken into consideration as soon as possible, and, for my part, I intend to give the hon. gentleman the best support I can. But, apart from those causes which are well known, and which are not objected to because they are clearly self-evident, is it not a fact that
9 p.m. the drainage of our Canadian products southward is also a cause of the high cost of living? At present milk, cream, fish, beef and potatoes are drained out of Canada by United States consumers. We were told, it is true, that the

United States market was of no consequence to Canada, but if we look at the exports to the United States during the last three or four months, we can see what are the effects of the jug-handled reciprocity which we are enjoying at present. I grant, Mr. Speaker, all the other causes of the high cost of living, but I say there is another, and that is the tariff-the food taxes. That cause is apparent; we can deal with it, and we can deal with it at the present session. Here are a few of the taxes which the Canadian consumer has to pay every time he sits down to a meal:	Canned
meats, 27J per cent; bread stuffs, 171 per cent; flour, 60 cents a barrel; fresh meats, 3 cents a pound; rice, 75 cents a quintal; sugar, $1.08 a quintal; oatmeal, 60 cents a quintal; eggs, 3 cents a dozen; butter, 4 cents a pound; cheese, 3 cents a pound; condensed milk, 3} cents a tin. This tariff on the food products appearing on the table of the workingman is a direct cause of the inflation of prices. Besides, the customs revenue tells the tale. We import foodstuffs from at least (fifty countries. During the year ended last March, Canada imported from the United States foodstuffs to the value of $23,072,100, on which duties amounting to $4,816,000, in round figures, were collected. From Great Britain foodstuffs to the value of $5,355,000 were imported, even with the British preference, the duties upon which amounted to $1,075,000. With respect to France and Germany the same applies, with a lower percentage of duty. So we are face to face with the fact that we pay duties on foodstuffs to the amount of more than $11,000,000 yearly, and this is one of the self-evident causes of the high cost of living. Speaking for myself only, and committing no one with whom I have the honour to be associated,
I say that I am ready to stand for the wiping out of all duties on the foodstuffs consumed in Canada. What has been good for the mother country; what is good for the American consumer at the present time, is good enough for me, a Canadian.
But we are asked: Are you going to deprive the farmer, who is, after all, perhaps the greatest producer in our country, of the little protection which he now enjoys? But is he not also a consumer? The articles of which I have given a list, and on which duties are paid, are consumed as well by the farmer as by the workingman, and if the duties on these articles are wiped out, the farmer will benefit by it. But, Mr. Speaker, when protection is concerned, you can always make an argument if

you wish to fasten and tighten around the neck of the farmer the collar of serfdom. In this conflict of opinion as to the removal of food taxes, who is the best judge, after all? Canada, thank Heaven, is a great farming community; Canada and the Canadian West is one of Nature's greatest farms and the Canadian grain growers and grangers fairly represent, I think, those classes of industry. What did the grain growers advocate, the farmers of the great prairie provinces west of Lake Superior, and even the farmers of the province of Ontario? First and foremost, larger markets for western wheat. Next, free interchange of foodstuffs and agricultural implements, free cement, free lumber, increase of the British preference to fifty per cent, and free trade with Great Britain within five years. I, for one, do not say that all this can be granted at one fell swoop, but I do say that free wheat, at least, which is being sought by both the political parties in Western Canada, should be granted by the Government. We were told this afternoon by the genial member for Dundas (Mr. Broder) that, like that American with the eye of a cat, we see nothing but rats and mice around us. Let us see what rats and mice the grain growers saw, the men whom you are so anxious to protect? Let me quote a few crisp sentences from the memorial presented by the grain growers when last they came to Ottawa.
Expansion in farming operations has ceased. Uess than 100,000 acres has been broken in 1913, as against an estimate of 4,000,000 two years previous; and this in the face of the fact that upwards of . half a million immigrants have been brought into that western country within the last three years.
The last two years have demonstrated that western farmers are not going to continue to grow crops at a loss. They cannot grow grain at a profit in larger quantities without other markets and alternate route for shipment. So long as our grain is forced to go for export through one channel that lends itself so readily to the manipulation of grain speculation, and the Imposing of excessive freight charges by combinations of transportation companies, we need look for no great increase in production.
In the four years, 1908 to 1911, when the growth of the West was at its height, the crop area increased from 8,312,956 acres in 1908 to 17,488,117, in 1911. The next two years showed a decrease of 1,259,617, and It remains with this Government to say whether we revert to this rapid growth of the decade ending 1911, or remain as we have since.
We submit that the wider market afforded us by accepting the offer of the United States for free interchange of natural products would have the same effect in stimulating the raising of wheat, oats, barley and flax as free access to the United States market for cattle has already done for that line of farm enterprise. Not only because it would provide another market for grain, but also because it would provide a competitive route for transporting grain to Europe.
We ask that all food stuffs be placed on the free list as we believe that the taxing of food is a crime against humanity.
The sensible thing for the Canadian people to do is to stop borrowing money, pay for what we buy and produce for export to meet our obligations.
Wherein should we tax the benefit of money invested in agriculture for the benefit of capital invested in manufacturing?
A few men become millionaires, while the masses become poorer; a few live in mansions, while many are forced into slums.
Manufacturing is unduly expanding, while the farming industry languishes because of being drained of its life blood. *
Farmers do not object to pay their share of the cost of Government. They are willing to submit to any system that will be of equitable taxation, levied for revenue purposes only.
That is the situation as described by the very farmers whom the Government is so anxious to protect. I was reading the other day a Life of John Bright, written by a nephew of Macaulay, Mr. Trevelyan. It is the latest biography of John Bright, and with your permission, Mr. Speaker, I would like to read a short passage from that work, describing the condition of the people in England at the time of the repeal of the Corn Laws. It seems to me that there is a close analogy between the condition he describes and the one described in the memorial left in the hands of the Government by the grain growers and the grangers of the West. It reads as follows:-
We your petitioners, dwell in a land whose merchants are noted for their enterprise, whose manufacturers are very skilful, and whose workmen are proverbial for their industry. The land itself is goodly, the soil rich, and the temperature wholesome. It is abundantly furnished with materials of commerce and trade; it has numerous and convenient harbours; in facility of internal communication it exceeds all others. For three and twenty years we have enjoyed a profound peace. Yet, with all these elements of national prosperity, and with every disposition and capacity to take advantage of them, we find ourselves overwhelmed with public and private suffering. We are bowed down under a load of taxes; our traders are trembling on the verge of bankruptcy; our workmen are starving; capital brings no profit and labour no remuneration; the home of the artificer is desolate, and the warehouse of the pawnbroker is full; the workhouse is crowded and the manufactory is deserted. We have looked on every side, we have searched diligently in order to find out the causes of a distress so sore and so long continued. We can discover none in nature or in Providence. Heaven has dealt graciously by the people; but the foolishness of our rulers has made the goodness of God of none effect.

My hon. friend, the
radical, does not seem to !be a great believer in what I am expressing now. He may have occasion to speak later on in the debate, but, this, at least is my opinion. Having dealt with the currency system President Wilson is now dealing with the trusts and mergers, one of the causes of the high cost of living. It is useless to mince matters, it is just as well to speak plainly and honestly to the privileged class, who, since 1879, have been enjoying their privileges. Contrast the attitude of the President of the United States as regards trusts and mergers with that of the Canadian Government. The President presented the case, he said ' as it lies in the thought of the country/ reiterating 'that private monopoly is indefensible and intolerable,' and declaring that conscientious men throughout the nation would not be satisfied until practices now deprecated by public opinion as restraints of trade and commerce were corrected. ' We are now about to write the additional articles of our constitution of peace ', said the President. ' The peace that is honour and freedom and prosperity.' Besides suggesting the scope of legislation, the President made a personal appeal for an atmosphere of friendliness and co-operation in Congress while handling the problem. Then the points of the new legislation are given, but I need not recite them, because they appear in the public prints. Contrast, Sir, the attitude of the President of the United States as regards the trusts, combines and mergers with the attitude of the present hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers). We have in the memorial of the Grain-growers' Association a direct attack on the combines, the mergers, and the monopolies existing in Canada; we heard last year authoritative statements with reference to them from the hon. the Labour member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville); we heard the member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) the other day unveiling the famous lake steamship merger, and we all remember the case of the United 'Shoe Machinery Company. Some years ago the Liberal Government passed a Combines Investigation Act and the first combine to come under the operation of that legislation was the United Shoe Machinery Company. In May, 1910, the Hon. Mackenzie King, then Minister of Labour, introduced the legislation, and, some time afterwards various complaints were made by the manufacturers of boots 13
and shoes in Canada, that their business was hampered and made unduly costly by the trade methods of the United Shoe Machinery Company of Canada. It was alleged that the company, which was an adjunct of the United Shoe Machinery Company of the United States, was a perfect sample of a combine in restraint of trade. A board was appointed over which Mr. Justice Lau-rendeau (now the city attorney for Montreal) presided, and on October 20, 1912, that board reported:
The United Shoe Machinery Company is a combine, and by,the operation of the clauses of the lease quoted in the foregoing, which restricts the use of the leased machinery in the way therein set forth; competition in the manufacture, production, sale, and supply of shoe machinery in Canada has been and is unduly restricted and prevented.
To make a long story short, the board reported against the United Shoe Machinery Oompany, and the company was liable, according to the law passed in 1910, to a fine of $1,000 per day. In the month of November last, I find in the Labour Gazette, the report of the Deputy Minister of Labour dated July 15, 1913. After citing facts it concludes with the following significant statement:
The Board's report having been published in the Canada Gazette of October 26, 1912, the date on which the company would be subject to the operation of section 23 was advanced to May 6, 1913 and thereafter. 1 do not see the Minister of Labour in his seat but I am quite sure the United Shoe Machinery Company is still at liberty to uphold its combine, and to restrict trade and supply in Canada according to its sweet will. Again, I say: contrast the attitude of the President of the United States with the attitude of the Canadian Minister of Labour-

Mr.- LEMIEUX: I have given the date of the report published in the Canada Gazette. What have they done since, anyway? I am told that they have done nothing, and that the combine still exists. If the legislation passed by the ex-Minister of Labour, Mr. Mackenzie King, is not elastic enough, and the Solicitor General- representing the West as he does and representing it very creditably-is anxious that this combine should be destroyed, why does he not employ his legal acumen to implement that legislation?
