The Minister of Finance, after surveying the whole situation, gave rather drastic advice to the farmers of this country. He

said to the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald): Do not be a bear on Canadian conditions, and he told the farmers to be possessed of rational optimism. The Minister of Finance told us: We are going to educate the farmers; we will make the farmers increase their production, and everything after that will go on smoothly. Sir, I can anticipate the answer of the farmers to the candid advice given by such a candid friend as the Minister of Finance; I know that the answer of the farmers will be: Give us wider markets; give us free food, free wheat, free agricultural implements, and make war on the trusts and the combines and the monopolies. The Minister of Finance spoke with sarcasm about the famous Cobden metal, but I would point out to him that Cobden and Bright captured England some sixty years ago by appealing to the common sense of the people, and not to prejudices. I for one do not care to catechise in this House, but it is not bad, perhaps it is even *quite opportune that we should retain the fundamentals on this question of the producer and the consumer. In reading the diary of John Bright on the existence of monopolies in England, I find the following wholesome truisms. He says:
Monopoly presupposes some advantage, to those who possess it. It gives to them the protection of the market and excludes foreign grown corn in order that in a market insufficiently supplied they may obtain a higher price than their corn is really worth. This higher price can only be obtained by preventing the food market being as abundantly supplied as it would be if the regular laws of commerce were not interfered with. This higher price therefore exists and is procurable only from the existence of scarcity intentionally created by law.
This is a wholesome truth propounded by John Bright, quite an authority on the matter and quite a friend of the common people who, to use the words of Abraham Lincoln, must be really loved by the Almighty as they are so numerous. Mr. Bright goes on to say:
This increased value places the food out of the reach of those whose means are most limited, whilst the most wealthy classes are still able to procure as much as they require. The pressure of scarcity comes then upon the poorest portion of the people. In a besieged city the rich and powerful can hold out longest-[DOT]
For instance, the noble eighteen could hold longest against the fifteen thousand asking Mayor Hocken for free bread and free soup.
[DOT]-the poor and defenceless feel famine soonest This law-made famine is unequal, sparing the rich and crushing the poor.

That is the story of the bread rioters in Regina.
Famine on board a ship at sea would be equally borne by all. Admiral and cabin-boy would share the biscuits, but as the Corn Law scarcity is created for the special benefit of one class, it is but likely that all the suffering should be averted from that class. The scarcity affects various portions of the community, in the inverse ratio of their power to endure it. The labourers probably are the only class that feel it in a positive insufficiency of food, and of these the weakest and poorest, whose labour is least valuable and least skilled, bear the greatest intensity of suffering.
Perhaps this may appear a little out of date, and I hear sneers from some of my hon. friends on the other side. But who will dare deny that in this young country of ours we are face to face, in Winnipeg, in Vancottver, in Toronto, in Montreal with slums and with people underfed? If you read the morning press, you will find that clergymen from nearly all the great cities are clamouring to-day in favour of the underfed and against the slums. Though the fundamentals may be a little out of date, though I may appear a little archaic in my economic, notions, yet I believe that it is well for Canada that someone should rise in the House of Commons and speak the language of tiuth, commonsense and justice to the monopolists who have enjoyed their privileges during thirty or forty years. Oh! but we are told, that the right hon. the leader of the Opposition has changed his policy. He was first of all for free trade as we have it in England. Then he was for a continental union. Then he was for unrestricted reciprocity. Then he was for readjustment of the tariff; finally he became in favour of restricted reciprocity, and now he is a free fooder for the moment, as said with smile the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. White). Say what you like, take the whole course of the right hon. gentleman's career, whether he advocated continental union-and it is not proven-whether he fought for unrestricted reciprocity-and unrestricted reciprocity found favour even in Ontario in 1891-though he was for free trade as we have it in England, for restricted reciprocity, though he is to-day in favour of free food, there is something of consistency in his stand-he is for the reduction of taxation. He is not for the increase of taxation and the consolidation of monopolies, combines and mergers. Permit me to quote one phrase of Sir Robert Peel's letter to a friend of his. He, too was considered as a great apostate, because he stood for the people against the big interests.
Some of the masses even were against him as they were against Cobden and Bright.
In a letter, which a friend of mine read in the British Museum and which he copied three or four years ago, because it was in his own handwriting, I found the following phrase which applies very well to the right hon. the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier):
I have many difficulties to contend with r much misrepresentation and obloquy to encounter on the part of those whom I verily believe I am protecting from evils and dangers , of which they seem little aware.
When the right hon. gentleman disappears from public life-and I trust that this is a far-off contingency-he may well say, with Sir Robert Peel:
I shall leave a name execrated by every monopolist who maintains perfection for his own individual benefit, but it may be, I shall leave a name sometimes remembered with expressions of good will, in those places that are the abodes of men whose lot it is to labour and to earn their bread by the sweat of their brow.
Nothing has been said about the naval question, and possibly this is the cause of the nervousness of the Postmaster General. The naval question, much to your surprise, Mr. Speaker, perhaps much to your comfort, is now amongst the departed. The hearse that took the Naval Bill from this House to the Upper Chamber left, the corpse where it should remain. The naval question has been shelved by the Government. I will not recite the various phases of the naval question, although I am tempted to do so by the presence in this Chamber to-day of the author of the far-famed resolution of 1909. We know, first, that this motion was introduced in 1909 in favour of a Canadian navy. We know, further, that it was made unanimous. We know, also, that the right hon. leader of the Government (Mr. Borden) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) in their speeches in the House of Commons, in England, at Halifax and in Ontario, favoured a Canadian navy as per the resolution of 1909. We know that the Drummond and Artha-baska election took place in 1910. It was found out, perhaps by the former Minister of Public Works (Mr. Monk), that the Liberals' difficulties were the Tories' opportunity. We know that it was through the election in Drummond and Arthabaska that the Tories had their first vision of a victory. We know the contradictory attitudes taken by the ex-Minister of Public Works in the province of Quebec, and by

the then leader of the Opposition (Mr. Borden) in the English-speaking provinces of the Dominion. We know that in the campaign of 1911 the Tory jingoes were paying -yes, I have it on the authority of Mr. Bourassa over his own signature-the Tory jingoes of Montreal and Toronto were paying for the sowing of the Nationalist seed in Canada. We know what happened; we were defeated, of course. The first session took place. My hon. friend the Prime Minister was feeling his ground. Would he repeal the Naval Bill? Would he introduce a new naval policy?-the Tory jingo policy of centralization as against the policy of my right hon. friend the present leader of the Opposition? The Prime Minister went to England, accompanied by his fervent home ruler, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), and by that fervent Nationalist-of that time-the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier). When they came back a banquet took place in Montreal at the Windsor hotel, and we are familiar with the declarations made By the Prime Minister. He told his hearers: I have my information from the proper sources, I have consulted the Admiralty; the House will convene in a few weeks; I shall submit my naval policy to the faithful Commons of Canada, and if Parliament prove unfaithful, I will appeal to the people of Canada. The emergency appeared on the 5th of December, 1913. We remember the heroic resistance of the Reform party against the tyranny and the stampede of the jingo party. We are aware of the effect, the damaging effect, of Mr. Churchill's letter. We had closure-'a good French word misused for a very bad thing; closure was introduced under the master hand of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers). We know what was the answer of the Senate to the action of the majority in the House of Commons. While not referring at all : to the little incident before our Easter duties of last year, now that the atmosphere of the House of Commons is serene and peaceful -is it not a fact, Sir, that events which took place since last session have vindicated the course of the Canadian Liberal party? I listened to the lecture at the Canadian Club in this city on Saturday by Mr. J. S. Ewart. We may differ as regards Mr. Ewart. He is an independent; he is above party politics. But as regards his perfect knowledge of the affairs of the British Empire, I think we can all take Mr. Ewart's word. Read that lecture of Mr. Ewart's, and read it again. He tells us that since last session the Australian navy is an accomplished fact, the Australian navy with the Australian flag at its mastheads. Since last session New Zealand has started a navy. Since last session-when my hon. friend from Brandon (Mr. Aikins) on his return from Europe declared that war was actually in existence between England and Germany-there has been a rapprochement between England and Germany. And if you look at the Annual Register for last year, you will find that the best customer that John Bull has is Germany. So far, then, our course has been vindicated since last session. More than that, the policy propounded by the Conservative party in this House-I should say the policy re-echoed by the Conservative party in this House, for that policy was imposed on the Prime Minister of Canada by Mr. Churchill, by the clerks of the Admiralty and by the party of centralization in England-the best authorities amongst the Imperialists in England, Imperialists of the sanest kind, men like Mr. Richard Jebb, Admiral Henderson and Admiral Fremantle, have declared that the policy propounded by the right hon. leader of the Opposition was the only good policy for Canada and for the empire. I shall not weary the House with quotations, but I repeat-Sir Richard Jebb, one of the best known apostles of the Imperial gospel, a disciple of Mr. Chamberlain and Lord Milner, Admiral He iderson and Admiral Fremantle have declared that the time has come to accept the policy of the leader of the Canadian Opposition. More than that, the London Times, the Thunderer-inspired at times-has approved of the Australian navy and the New Zealand navy. By that admission it has approved of the Canadian navy. But it had approved of the Canadian navy before. As I say, I do not care to weary the House with old extracts, but after the Conference of 1911, the Times shouted with joy at the announcement that at last there was to be a great Imperial policy based on the declaration made by the one who had been singled out in that Conference by Mr. Asquith as the Nestor of the Conference-namely Imperial unity based on local autonomy. Sir, the naval question has been shelved; the emergency has disappeared, and the time is now ripe for a permanent policy. As a Liberal, and as a loyal Canadian, I say to the Government, now that the emergency has disappeared, bring down a permanent policy; let it be along the lines of the Australian policy, and you will find the Canadian Liberal party with the Government, and supporting that policy. The emergency has disappeared but the Gio-

conda has also disappeared from Paris. I suspect that some fine Italian hand will some day sooner or later bring back the Mona Lisa of the Tory party, the emergency. When will it be restored and adorn the walls of this Parliament? Mr. Speaker, you need not guess it; we all know it. The emergency invented last year and shelved this year will be restored as soon as there are any rumours of a general election. It is needed for the flag-waving campaign. The ' no truck, no trade ' cry is now too old a song; the cry of ' Canada as an adjunct of the United States ' is dead and buried, and a new patented flag-waving campaign is needed to re.urn the Tory party to office. But the ' wolf, wolf ' cry will not succeed a secand time. I know that certain jingo papers are trying to make themselves believe that there is an emergency. It must not die, it must not disappear. I read in the Montreal Star of Saturday the following lines:
The airy manner in which Sir Wilfrid Daurier dismissed all question of a naval ' emergency ' -past, present or future-the other day in Parliament, passed the comprehension of those who take an intelligent interest in foreign politics. The proofs of an ' emergency ' are so plain, so plentiful, so painfully omnipresent, that it is incomprehensible to men who bother with anything outside their own bailliwick how a statesman of Sir Wilfrid's stature could possibly blind his eyes to what is written in massed bayonets across the continent of Europe.
I wonder if the gentleman who in his sound sober sense wrote the above lines is one of that organization of crooks described by Lord Welby, who uses the following language:
We are in the hands of an organization of crooks. They are politicans, generals, manufacturers of armaments, and journalists, all of them anxious for unlimited expenditure and given to inventing scares which terrify the public and terrify ministers of the Crown.
I am quite positive, Mr. Speaker-and I am sincere in this-that the gentleman who said that the emergency was written in massed bayonets intended to terrify my hon. friend the Minister of
10 p.m. Public Works. Lord Welby continues that he could remember six war scares, each one made to order, and in each case of which the public had been gulled. Each time the scare had been exposed later on, but each new scare took, and resulted in enormous expenditure on armaments. These, are the utterances of Lord Welby, a member of that august assembly, the House of Lords, which was reformed by Lloyd George, the much-talked
of minister who has himself advocated a reduction in armament. I would not for one moment leave the House with the impression that Lord Welby is a crank, and that he did not know what he was talking about. I hold in my hand a little blue book-not the blue book which the Government intends to give as bread to the consumers of Canada, the report of the investigation of the high cost of living commission, but a little book bearing the suggestive tittle:	' The Six Panics and Other
Essays,' by F. W. Hirst. Mr. Hirst, as we all know is the financial authority of the British Empire. He is the editor of the London Economist, a paper which is eagerly read every time it reaches his office by the Minister of Finance in Canada. Mr. Hirst is no crank; he is a good Britisher. Of course he has a little failing: he is a Radical. 1 commend the reading of his book to every member of the House of Commons. There were six panics in England during the last century. The first lasted from 1847 to 1848, and it originated by a letter of the Duke of Wellington. It was addressed to a British officer, and afforded painful evidence of enfeebled naval power. The iron duke, speaking about the painful evidence of enfeebled power of the naval forces of Great Britain, naturally excited public opinion, and the people were led to believe that the French were going to invade England. Mr. Hirst explained how tile panic ended:
This panic ended dramatically. Lord Russell was Chancellor of the Exchequer, and the Budget produced on February 18, 1848, raised the income tax from sevenpence to a shilling in the pound, in order to increase armaments and to reorganize the militia in accordance with the Duke of Wellington's advice. When this addition to taxation came into view, in association with preparations against the danger of invasion, the danger seemed to diminish and the panic abated.
And strange to say, a few weeks afterwards the invader entered England, but it was the aged French King Louis Philippe who went to England not as an invader but as a refugee. He had lost the crown of France. The second panic-again a French panic-lasted from 1851 to 1853. Lord John Russell, speaking in the House of Commons, said:
Really, to hear or read some of the letters, some of the language used by some portion of the press, one would imagine that these two great nations, so wealthy, so similar in enlightenment, were going to butcher one another, merely to try what would be the effect of percussion caps and needle guns.
Mr. Joseph Hume, the veteran economist, describes the condition in England in one of the debates as follows:

Our present panics are not due as in times past to the old women, but to our having too many clubs about London, containing so many half pay officers, who have nothing to do but to look about for themselves and their friends. These are the people who write to the newspapers anxious to bring grist to the mill somehow or other.
And you know how the panic ended.
The alarm was constantly stimulated by startling paragraphs in the newspapers. One day the French army at Rome was reported to be chafing and dissatisfied, because it could not share in the invasion of England and the sack of London; the next there were whispered revelations of a secret plan, divulged by General Changarnier, for invading England and seizing the metropolis (which he publicly contradicted) then we were told of a plot for securing a naval station in the West Indies: next, the French Government had sent an order for steam frigates to Messrs. Napier of Glasgow.
Admirals on half pay were every morning surveying the channel and seeing on the horizon the French frigates coming with the invaders. How did the panic end? Mr. Hirst tells us that a little arrangement took place between the War Office in London and the War Office in Paris and the panic ended by the union of the French and English armies for aggression in the Crimea. The third panic lasted from 1859 to 1861. It was again a French invasion scare but Richard Cobden published at that time a little book entitled, The Three Panics, That ended the scare. There was another panic in 1884. Mr. Hirst tells us how it started.
According to an old official of the Admiralty this first success of ' the advanced school of naval thought ' was one ' most unexpected ' and owed its origin to the merest accident. Lord Salisbury the Conservative leader on a visit to Portsmouth in the summer of 1884 had heard discontent expressed about the state of the navy by some of the officials there and referred to the matter in a speech, which seemed to express a doubt as to whether the navy was strong enough to ensure the national safety.
A few days afterwards the question was taken up by Mr. Stead, the journalist. The Annual Register, alluding to him, remarked:
In nearly all quarters the Government's answer to the popular demand was pronounced inadequate. Nevertheless there arose a few anti-alarmists or skeptics who declared that the outcry in the newspapers was chiefly, if not wholly, the work of the professional advisers of the Admiralty, assisted in a great measure by the large ship builders, whose yards were empty and whose trade was temporarily at a standstill.
And the fifth panic was called the dreadnought scare. I need not worry the House with that. We all know that when Sir
Henry Campbell Bannerman became Prime Minister he reduced the expenditure on the Navy Bill by many million pounds. Immediately the shipbuilders and armour platers raised a row and a campaign was started in the press to get England to build dreadnoughts. England had already one at the time, but as Germany was contemplating the building of many dreadnoughts, England was urged to start building them too. We all remember, too, the Blatchford scare and the articles written by that famous Socialist. We remember too that farce, humiliating for England, which was played all over England and even in the city of Ottawa-an Englishman's Home. You remember the lines, Mr. Speaker.
We want eight-
We won't waitdreadnoughts. Thanks to Mr. Hirst, we all know now the source of the dreadnought scare. It was started and paid for 'by the armour platers and we know how ultimately it failed. But we had another panic not so very long ago. We can have no more panics about dreadnoughts and superdreadnoughts, but not many weeks ago we were terrified by an air-ship panic. Officers on half pay I suppose, had seen lights in the firmament that were neither stars nor meteors; surely they must be the lights of the Zeppelins. And the press immediately started a campaign for supplying the home Government with airships. They succeeded. This is what Mr. Hirst says:
Previously, on February 20, this business side of the agitation came to the surface in a news column (headed * Aeroplane Purchases- Machines for the British Army and Navy') which runs as follows:
And he then gives the number of machines bought by the English Government at the instigation of a few comedians writing in the press for the airship firms. Mr. Speaker, I have said enough on this subject. We in Canada have been for the last few years the laughing stock of the armour platers and of the insincere jingoes. I admit that many, in fact the majority of the jingoes, act in good faith but there is too much jingoism in Canada; too many people believe that they are born to save the empire. Mr. Asquith, the Prime Minister of England, can be depended upon in matters Imperial. In 1911 he served us with a notice in his answer to Sir Joseph Ward. He said that never so long as he was Prime Minister of England would the foreign policies of Great Britain be controlled by the overseas do-

minions. That was a notice very courteously and very firmly served on the empire savers. Mr. Asquith will not abdicate even for the prime ministers of Canada, Australia and New Zealand. He with Sir Edward Grey, is the inspirer responsible for the foreign policy of Great Britain and he does not intend * to abdicate his functions. We have besides, it seems to me, our own problems, we have our own difficulties; we have the tariff to deal with, the labour question to deal with, we have the Hindu agitation in British Columbia to look after, and we have the yellow immigration to cope with. These are problems, these are difficulties, which can well occupy the time of the ministers of the Crown in Canada. Let us therefore turn our attention to Canadian affairs. We should not be ashamed to deal with Canadian affairs. We are building up our country. The mandate of the Prime Minister of Canada is the Dominion's mandate, not the empire's mandate. Serving Canada is serving the Empire.
Too much militarism in this country! Militarism is not a healthy condition. I believe in a moderate military expenditure. I believe that the common people of this country are ready to bear their share of military expenditure, but, Mr. Speaker-the rides-the joy rides-of my hon. friend the Minister of Militia (Mr. Hughes) in Europe with his gold-plated staff, his antics, his hiring of automobiles at $25 a day, is indeed a very poor advertisement abroad for our young country. The expenditure is out of all proportion. If I may be allowed I will again quote John Bright:
I do not care for military greatness or military renown. I care for the condition of the people among whom I live. Palaces, baronial castles, great halls, stately mansions, do not make a nation. The nation in every country dwells in a cottage and unless the light of your constitution can shine there, unless the beauty of your legislation and the excellence of your statesmanship are impressed there on the feeling and condition of the people, rely upon it you have yet to learn the duties of government.
The hon. Minister of Finance is shrugging his shoulders:	Well, we won the by-elections anyway; we won six out of seven. I have here the circulars which were distributed in the county of Chateauguay, where, as my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) has said, a double appeal was made. I know that the farmers were told to vote for the Government because the Government would give them road money and the French-Canadians in the county of Chateauguay were told what, by the Deputy
Speaker? Mr. Speaker, I might inform you, en passant, that your deputy was in that election contrary to all precedent, and he was there holding public meetings. The great constitutional party respecting old usages and customs! Well, Sir, he was there distributing circulars telling what?
Mr. Borden is the friend of the province of Quebec. Never have we been so well treated as since he has been Prime Minister. Contrast that with the Laurier regime.
By the way, Mr. Speaker, you remember what the Mail said about Laurier being so lavish with the province of Quebec and so stingy with Ontario?
Contrast with the Laurier regime the attitude of Mr. Rogers. He is more generous with the province in the distribution of public works than was Mr. Pugsley, the Liberal minister, thirteen million dollars of public money comes in one year. There are public works for all over the province. Twenty-five million dollars will be expended by the Borden Government in the province of Quebec this year.
Then follows the words, ' eloquent figures.' We have here the figures for wharfs and rivers and the Quebec harbour. My hon. friend the Postmaster General thinks a little of Quebec. Here are the appropriations in the Main and Supplementary Estimates for harbours and river improvements. Here we find in high headlines:	Quebec,

Then there is this appeal:
Electors of Chateauguay, will you return to the Brodeur-Lemieux regime, or do you prefer the regime of Mr. Rogers and prosperity for
the province of Quebec?
Then we find also the following:
Mr. Borden is fair with the French-Canadians. We have rather a large portion of patronage.
I am afraid that is an appeal to the appetites of the people. What do you think, Mr. Speaker, of the action of your Deputy Speaker? Let us row read another leaflet:

Since Mr. Borden has been made Premier, the province of Quebec is much better treated than under the Liberal regime.
I hope the Mail will publish that.
Mr. Laurier used to neglect his countrymen because he used to say that on account of his nationality he could not do as much for them, but under the Conservatives we have two judges on the Supreme Court. Mr. Laurier has left us with one, Mr. Brodeur, who is the weaker of the two. Sir Rlzear Taschereau has been succeeded by Mr. Fitzpatrick. When Mr. Gobeil, Deputy Minister of Public Works, took his pension, Mr. Laurier replaced him by Mr. J. B. Hunter, an Englishman. And -when Mr. Gourdeau left his office as Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries, Mr. Laurier appointed Mr. Johnston, of Cape Breton, another Englishman. From 1896 to 1911 the Laurier Government did nothing for the harbour of Quebec, but it suent millions for the harbours of Ontario and the Northwest.
Much better to have an English-Canadian as a prime minister than a French-Canadian as Laurier was. Since Mr. Borden has been in office he has shown the greatest sympathy for the French-Canadian ; he loves our race.
Then there is quoted a few phrases from a speech delivered in the House of Commons on the 22nd of March, 1905; it is too long to translate, but it is no doubt very eloquent and it does justice to Mr. Borden's broadmindedness. The article goes on to say:
The Borden Government has shown by acts
that it respects our race. Is it not true-
Oh, Mr. Speaker, I come to you now; this is for your benefit:
Is it not true that 15 French-Canadian translators for the blue books have been appointed this year after having passed examinations? Even Liberals have been appointed. It is because Mr. Borden wants to be just to our language that he ordered these appointments.
In spite of you, Mr. Speaker.
Under Mr. Laurier it was impossible to have blue books in French until two years after their publication in the English version. Why should we not be just towards Mr. Borden when he is such a good fellow, especially when he gives us what Mr. Laurier has so often refused? Under the Liberals there was but one judge at the Exchequer Court, the Hon. Mr. * Justice Cassels. Is it not true that Mr. Borden has appointed another one, the Hon. Mr. Audette, a French-Canadian? Why should we not recognize such acts of justice? Since Mr. Doherty has been Minister of Justice he has appointed in his department two French-Canadian lawyers, Messrs. Beauchesne and De-Salabery. All the lawyers in the province of Quebec who have done business with Mr. Doherty for the past two years know that there is very serious amelioration in that direction. Mr. Borden has appointed a Senator from Nova Scotia, Mr. Girroir, a French-Aeadian from Antigonish who had been mentioned to Mr. Borden by the Acadian leaders themselves. Mr. Borden has appointed as Chairman of the
fMr. Lemieux.]
Joint Waterways Commission the Hon. T. C. Casgrain, a French-Canadian, and that appointment is really quite creditable. Thus is it with all important posts in the civil service; we have our large share of patronage. We receive much more since the last two years than we have over received during the whole tenure of office of Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
The Minister of Finance said: ' We won the election in Chateauguay.' Yes, Mr. Speaker, they won the election, but I give you the means by which they won that election in Chateauguay. The Minister of Finance, 1 know, is a bookworm, and he is fond of Napoleonic literature. Not very long ago I read new memoirs describing the campaign of Napoleon in Russia, and I saw related there that as the army of Napoleon, made up of soldiers and adventurers from all the countries of Europe- French, Spaniards, Prussians, Italians, Austrians-as that army entered the great solitudes of Russia some of Napoleon's staff of generals met an old Russian pope and conversation ensued between the humble Russian and the several invading generals arrayed in uniforms glittering in gold. They told the poor old man that they were sure of reaching Moscow, that they were confident to defeat the Russians, and that the army of Napoleon would triump after a brief campaign. And the old Russian said to one of the staff; general, you will cross with your magnificent army of adventurers the Beresina and you may cross the Niemen, and you will possibilv reach Moscow, but count your troops and your eagles as you advance, and count them again as you come back.
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister is also on his way to Moscow with his gorgeously uniformed general, the Minister of Militia. In the ranks of the Tory party are to be found men of all stripes; we find some of the eighteen insurgent capitalists represented by the Minister of Finance; here are the loyal Orangemen and there, the pious Ultramontane -look at him just facing me now. I see in that army stalwart Tories, plenty of them, jingoes and Nationalist musketeers. They have passed two sessions and we are entering on a third. We may have a fourth session, but some day, the general elections will come. Napoleon with his generals and his adventurers went into the solitudes of Russia after Ulm, Friedland and Jena, and they crossed the Beresina and they crossed the Niemen, but his ragged remnants of a once grand army had to recross these rivers in their retreat, and they had to meet Wellington at Waterloo.

The Tory army may cross tlieir Beresina and their Niemen, but the e'ections will come, sooner or later, and they will soon have to face their Wellington, and, at the same time, meet their Waterloo.

I suppose I will not disappoint
the House if I say that I have no intention of speaking at such length as my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux). The hon. gentleman has spoken for three and a half hours. I shall not judge the matter of his speech, because it might be thought by some who know that we have not been very intimate friends in the past, that my judgment is prejudiced. However, I venture to say that I do not think it will take me one-quarter of the time to travel over the same ground and to place the facts as they really are, not as he imagines them to be. It is not expected that the House should sit very late to-night, and consequently I move the adjournment of the debate.
